title: Shaun of the Dead
logline: Simon Pegg and Nick Frost ride out a zombie apocalypse at the pub. Tightly plotted British genre comedy built on callbacks.
overview: Shaun lives a supremely uneventful life, which revolves around his girlfriend, his mother, and, above all, his local pub. This gentle routine is threatened when the dead return to life and make strenuous attempts to snack on ordinary Londoners.

jokes.text: Liz tries to have a heartfelt conversation about needing more couple time; Ed punctuates every pause with 'Fuck,' 'Bollocks,' 'Cock it' while playing a video game, completely oblivious
jokes.setup: Liz is mid-earnest relationship speech asking for more alone time with Shaun
jokes.punchline: Ed interjects 'Fuck... Bollocks... Cock it' in rapid succession, clearly reacting to a game and not the conversation
jokes.explanation: Earns its score because the interruptions are perfectly timed to the most emotionally loaded moments of Liz's speech. Ed isn't being rude on purpose — he's just completely in his own world — which is funnier and more character-specific than any intentional insult could be. The escalating vulgarity of the three words also gives it a satisfying mini-structure.

jokes.text: Shaun asks 'What do you mean?' and Ed responds asking what 'exacerbate' means instead
jokes.setup: Liz uses the word 'exacerbates' in a serious relationship conversation and Shaun asks 'What do you mean?'
jokes.punchline: Ed has been listening just enough to flag the vocabulary word, completely missing the emotional stakes: 'No, what does exacerbate mean?'
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy: one line does triple duty — reveals Ed's dim but earnest nature, deflates Liz's serious moment, and momentarily derails the whole conversation. The misdirection of Shaun's 'What do you mean?' setting up an answer about feelings but getting a vocabulary question is tight structural writing.

jokes.text: 'Can I get any of you cunts a drink?'
jokes.setup: An earnest group therapy-style conversation about Shaun and Liz's relationship and friend dynamics has been building; Ed has been peripheral and crass throughout
jokes.punchline: Ed wanders over with cheerful obliviousness and offers everyone a drink using the most offensively casual phrasing possible
jokes.explanation: One of the great single-line character comedy moments in the film. The word 'cunts' used as an affectionate plural while offering drinks is quintessentially Ed — aggressively laddish but completely without malice. Its timing (cutting through a solemn relationship conversation) and pitch-perfect delivery make it one of the most quotable lines in the reel. Character integration is near-perfect: no other character in any other film could deliver this line with the same innocent warmth.

jokes.text: David and Dianne's relationship: Daffs takes him to listed buildings, he drags her to theatre; 'I'm not so hot on theatre'
jokes.setup: Dianne is offering relationship advice about doing things together as a couple
jokes.punchline: Their own relationship is revealed as an equally mismatched compromise — she drags him to heritage sites, he forces her to theatre, and he quietly admits he doesn't even like the theatre
jokes.explanation: A functional background joke — the irony of the relationship-advice couple having their own quiet dysfunction is well-observed. 'I'm not so hot on theatre' lands as a mild, underplayed laugh. Not exceptional but serves good world-building comedy.

jokes.text: 'It was last week.' / 'Did you do anything special?' / 'We came here.'
jokes.setup: David asks if they did anything special for their anniversary
jokes.punchline: Shaun sheepishly admits they came to the same pub they always go to
jokes.explanation: Three-beat exchange with excellent economy. The escalating embarrassment — anniversary was last week, nothing special planned, and the special thing they did do was… come here — perfectly crystallises Shaun's arrested development without a single wasted word.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Listen to me. I'm beginning to sound like your mum.'
jokes.setup: Liz has been earnestly lecturing Shaun about growing up and taking initiative
jokes.punchline: She catches herself and notes the meta-irony — she sounds like his mother, whom she has never met
jokes.explanation: Works as a mild laugh and plants the 'not met his mum' detail that immediately pays off. Gets rewatch_bonus because on rewatch the mum thread becomes thematically important. The joke itself is competent but not particularly original.

jokes.text: Revelation that Liz has never met Shaun's mum after three years — 'Are you ashamed of your mum, Shaun?'
jokes.setup: Liz offhandedly mentions sounding like Shaun's mum; the group realises she has never met her
jokes.punchline: David piles on with 'Are you ashamed of your mum, Shaun?' — a perfectly pointed bit of social cruelty that deepens the picture of Shaun's dysfunction
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy escalation. David's social tone-deafness (or deliberate sharpness) in asking 'are you ashamed' is a good character beat and deepens the joke.

jokes.text: Ed: 'I love his mum.' / 'She's like butter' — instantly shut down
jokes.setup: Shaun defends his love for his mum during a cringe-y group interrogation
jokes.punchline: Ed announces he also loves Shaun's mum and starts singing a sexualised song about her, immediately cut off
jokes.explanation: Ed pivoting to a your-mum gag mid-serious moment is perfectly in character. The fact that he starts actually singing it — not just implying it — before being shut down gives it an extra beat of absurdist commitment. The 'Ed!' cutoff lands as its own comic beat.

jokes.text: 'Player two has entered the game.' — Ed arrives home during the day while Shaun is at work, implied via game announcement
jokes.setup: Shaun has just left for work; we cut to the flat
jokes.punchline: The video game announces 'Player two has entered the game' — Ed has come downstairs, implying he's been in bed all morning while Shaun worked
jokes.explanation: Elegant visual storytelling through a game audio cue: no dialogue needed to show that Ed does absolutely nothing all day. The game's formal announcement treating Ed's slothful descent as a 'player two entry' is a neat piece of cinematic comedy economy — a technique Edgar Wright uses throughout the film.

jokes.text: Pete's flat complaint: 'I'm not saying it was you.' Shaun: 'I know, man.' Pete: 'I'm saying it was Ed.'
jokes.setup: Pete starts diplomatically hedging about who left the front door open
jokes.punchline: He immediately abandons the diplomacy and directly accuses Ed in the same breath
jokes.explanation: The setup/punchline is a single breath long — the fake diplomatic hedge immediately punctured. Good economy, clean structure.

jokes.text: Pete: 'What? Dealing drugs?' / Shaun: 'He sells a bit of weed now and again. You've sold puff.' / Pete: 'Yeah, once. At college. To you.'
jokes.setup: Shaun defends Ed's contributions to the household ('he brings a bit in')
jokes.punchline: Pete reveals the hypocrisy: Shaun himself bought weed from Pete once, at college — so Pete has the moral high ground on exactly one deal
jokes.explanation: Three-step reveal with tight economy: Pete's indignant denial, the specificity of 'once, at college,' and the killer closer 'to you.' That final detail perfectly skewers Pete's self-righteousness. Good structure.

jokes.text: Pete: 'Because he can impersonate an orang-utan?' / Ed immediately: 'Fuck-a-doodle-doo.'
jokes.setup: Pete dismisses Ed's value to the household, sarcastically asking if the only thing Ed offers is an orang-utan impression
jokes.punchline: Ed immediately demonstrates it, delivering a garbled animal noise with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Earns its high score. The joke has a perfect three-part structure: (1) Pete's rhetorical put-down that invites no actual answer, (2) Ed's instant, unasked-for demonstration, and (3) the absurdity of 'Fuck-a-doodle-doo' as an orang-utan noise, which is the wrong animal sound entirely. Ed's total lack of shame or social reading makes this quintessentially Ed. 'Fuck-a-doodle-doo' is one of the most quotable single-unit jokes in the film.

jokes.text: Shaun's defence of Ed: 'That time we stayed up all night drinking apple schnapps and playing Tekken 2.' Pete: 'When was that?' Shaun: 'Five years ago.'
jokes.setup: Shaun claims Ed is 'a laugh' and can be 'pretty funny on occasion'
jokes.punchline: His sole supporting anecdote is five years old, involving apple schnapps and a PlayStation game — an inadvertent confession of arrested development
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the specificity ('apple schnapps,' 'Tekken 2') and the devastating reveal that the best memory Shaun can produce is half a decade old. Pete's flat 'When was that?' and the sheepish '...Five years ago' is a masterclass in timing via understatement.

jokes.text: Ed taking a drug phone call while Shaun tries to have a serious conversation with him
jokes.setup: Shaun attempts a sincere heart-to-heart with Ed about cleaning up and taking messages
jokes.punchline: Ed's phone rings mid-conversation and he casually handles a drug deal ('I've only got an 'enry meself') while Shaun talks at him
jokes.explanation: Ed's ability to talk to both Shaun and a drug customer simultaneously without registering any awkwardness is a good character joke. The gaming interjections ('Top left,' 'Reload,' 'Nice shot') layered on top make this a multi-track simultaneous-inattention gag.

jokes.text: Pete: 'It's not that taxing, is it? Writing something on a scrap of paper?' — delivered as rhetorical wisdom while Ed agrees to everything and does nothing
jokes.setup: Pete lectures Ed about the simple act of taking phone messages
jokes.punchline: Ed agrees to every instruction with monosyllabic 'Yep' and 'Nope,' making it clear he will do none of it
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy. The gap between Pete's reasonable expectations and Ed's complete disengagement is the joke. Gets the job done without being especially memorable.

jokes.text: Ed's repeated fart gag — 'I'll stop doing 'em when you stop laughing.' / 'I am not laughing.'
jokes.setup: Ed is apparently doing something gross/flatulent repeatedly; Shaun claims not to find it funny
jokes.punchline: Ed's self-justifying logic — 'I'll stop doing 'em when you stop laughing' — is delivered as genuine philosophy; Shaun's denial is undermined by context
jokes.explanation: The strength is in the relationship dynamic — Ed knows Shaun well enough to know he is secretly amused. It's warm and character-specific even if the base comedy (farting) is lowbrow. 'Oh my God, that's rotten' adds sensory texture.

jokes.text: 'Hey! You're dead.' — Ed kills Shaun in a video game immediately after Shaun gives him a sincere request
jokes.setup: Shaun has just finished a sincere ask for Ed to do what Pete said and do it 'for me'
jokes.punchline: Ed's immediate response is to announce Shaun is dead — in-game — with the same emotional register as if commenting on the relationship conversation
jokes.explanation: The ambiguity is the joke — 'Hey! You're dead' could be about the game or a commentary on Shaun's social life. Gets rewatch_bonus because on rewatch the 'dead' language resonates with the zombie premise the film is building toward.

jokes.text: Shaun takes a personal call in his own staff meeting while covering for the absent manager
jokes.setup: Shaun is mid-way through telling his team 'phones off, it's not a social gathering'
jokes.punchline: He immediately answers his own phone to chat with Ed's drug contact
jokes.explanation: The hypocrisy payoff is set up and delivered cleanly within a few lines. Shaun's authority evaporating the moment it is established is a good running theme for his character.

jokes.text: Shaun: 'There's no I in team but there is an I in pie.' / Beat. / 'In... there's an I in meat pie.' / 'The anagram of meat is team... I don't know what he's talking about.'
jokes.setup: Shaun tries to repeat his absent manager's motivational speech
jokes.punchline: He loses the thread mid-sentence, tries to salvage with 'meat pie,' then just confesses confusion in real time: 'I don't know what he's talking about'
jokes.explanation: One of the best set-piece jokes in the reel. The original mangled quote ('there is an I in pie') is already absurd, but the real comedy is in the live unravelling — Shaun trying to course-correct with 'meat pie,' discovering the anagram logic, and then simply giving up and expressing his own confusion while still leading the meeting. The structure mirrors real corporate-speech inanity and pays it off with beautiful self-awareness. 'I don't know what he's talking about' as a first-person confession about someone else's words is a genuinely clever comedic inversion.

jokes.text: Pete calls for phones off; Noel takes a call; Shaun snaps 'Keep your hair on, grandad' — then immediately asks how old Noel is
jokes.setup: Shaun reprimands Noel for using a phone after just doing it himself; Noel calls him 'grandad'
jokes.punchline: Shaun indignantly declares he's 29 — 'for Christ's sakes' — then asks how old Noel is; Noel: '17.' Shaun is speechless.
jokes.explanation: The age revelation lands because Shaun's indignant '29!' is immediately deflated — 29 vs 17 makes him sound even more like a grandad in a teenager's eyes. The 'When?' follow-up from Noel about Shaun's aspirations is an additional small knife-twist.

jokes.text: Shaun: 'I've got things I wanna do with my life.' Noel: 'When?'
jokes.setup: Shaun tries to frame himself as a man with ambition and future plans in front of a 17-year-old employee
jokes.punchline: Noel's one-word 'When?' devastates the aspiration entirely
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy: a single word joke. 'When?' is precisely the right word at precisely the right moment — it doesn't argue with Shaun, doesn't mock him, just asks the most devastating possible follow-up. Its placement after a beat makes it land harder. Near-perfect comedic economy.

jokes.text: 'You got red on you.' — customer's matter-of-fact observation about blood/ketchup on Shaun's shirt
jokes.setup: Shaun is mid-sales pitch for a TV package
jokes.punchline: A customer gestures to something red on Shaun's shirt, saying 'You got red on you' — played completely straight, as if it's a minor embarrassment rather than a zombie film omen
jokes.explanation: First instance of the film's signature running gag — 'You got red on you' — which will recur and gain meaning as zombie blood enters the picture. As a standalone line it's a mild observational joke; as a setup for a callback it's essential architecture. Gets rewatch_bonus because knowing viewers anticipate its return.

jokes.text: Philip's call: 'You haven't forgotten about tomorrow?' / 'Your bimonthly visit.' / 'You could bring the flowers you forgot on Mother's Day. I was gonna. / And not a cheap posy from a garage forecourt. I wasn't gonna.'
jokes.setup: Philip (Shaun's stepdad) rings during Shaun's sales pitch to remind him about a visit
jokes.punchline: Philip preemptively rebukes Shaun for things he hadn't done yet ('I was gonna') and defensively predicts what cheap option Shaun will choose; Shaun's denials get increasingly hollow
jokes.explanation: The 'I was gonna / I wasn't gonna' rhythm is excellent — Philip is so familiar with Shaun's shortcomings that he can pre-empt both the action and the specific cheap form it would take. This is rich relationship comedy. The 'garage forecourt' detail is exactly specific enough to be funny.

jokes.text: Philip ends the call: 'You've got red on you.'
jokes.setup: First 'you got red on you' was used by a stranger in the shop; Philip uses the exact same phrase to end a totally unrelated stepdad phone call
jokes.punchline: The repetition of the phrase by an entirely different person in a different context, still completely unexplained and unremarked upon
jokes.explanation: The second hit of the running gag, delivered so quickly after the first that the audience is still processing it. The fact that Philip — in a totally unrelated call — uses the exact same phrase is both a formal comedy escalation and the moment the gag becomes a proper running gag. The lack of explanation makes it funnier. It clearly scores above the first instance because now the pattern is established, which creates anticipation.

jokes.text: Noel: 'I thought it wasn't a social gathering?' — catching Shaun's hypocrisy about phone calls
jokes.setup: Shaun just told everyone phones off; he then took two personal calls back-to-back
jokes.punchline: Noel calls this out with the exact phrasing Shaun used
jokes.explanation: A reliable callback joke — the hypocrisy is already funny, the exact phrase repeat cements it. Not the most original structure but it executes cleanly.

jokes.text: Shaun's defence of stepdad call: 'A, he's not my dad, OK? He's my stepdad. And B, it was an emergency.' / Noel: 'What, like buying your mum some flowers?'
jokes.setup: Shaun tries to frame the stepdad call as a legitimate emergency
jokes.punchline: Noel deflates the 'emergency' by naming exactly what it was: being reminded to buy flowers
jokes.explanation: The 'A... and B' pomposity from Shaun is itself funny; the 'emergency = flowers' deflation from a 17-year-old is a satisfying puncture. The specificity of Noel remembering what the call was about adds to it.

jokes.text: Shaun: 'I do not find it difficult to keep my work and my social life separate.' — immediately answered by Liz calling his work phone
jokes.setup: Shaun pompously declares his work/life separation to Noel
jokes.punchline: His colleague immediately announces 'Shaun, it's Liz for you' — his girlfriend calling his work phone
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect setup/punchline structure — the boast and its immediate contradiction happen within seconds with no fat on the edit. The timing is the entire joke and Edgar Wright executes it with scalpel precision. The 'A and B' speech inflates the boast just enough to make the puncture land harder.

jokes.text: Shaun in the flower shop: 'They're for my mum.' / Florist: '"To a wonderful Mum" or "Supermum"?'
jokes.setup: Shaun sheepishly buys flowers, clarifying they're for his mum
jokes.punchline: He's forced to choose between two mawkish card options, landing on 'the first one' with zero enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Mild observational comedy about greeting card options. Functions as a beat more than a joke — it's setting up the later flower-to-Liz gag. The '...the first one' deadpan is the best element.

jokes.text: Yvonne: 'Glad somebody made it' — referring to Shaun and Liz still being together
jokes.setup: Shaun and Yvonne catch up; Yvonne learns he's still with Liz after three years
jokes.punchline: 'Glad somebody made it' — implying neither of them expected it, which is quietly damning
jokes.explanation: The backhanded compliment format is familiar but 'glad somebody made it' has the right level of casual brutality. Works as a small relationship comedy beat.

jokes.text: Shaun: 'Yeah...' — long pause — when asked if the restaurant is 'anywhere nice'; he clearly hasn't booked it
jokes.setup: Yvonne asks if the restaurant they're going to is 'anywhere nice'
jokes.punchline: Shaun's extended 'Yeah...' trails off, communicating that he has absolutely no idea because he hasn't made a reservation
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the silence/vagueness. A single elongated 'yeah' that trails into nothing is a perfectly economical way to communicate total incompetence without exposition. Simon Pegg's performance sells it and the film trusts the audience to read it.

jokes.text: Ed's 'tidy' flat: 'I had a few beers when I finished' — the flat looks worse than before
jokes.setup: Shaun comes home to find Ed proudly claiming he tidied up
jokes.punchline: The flat 'doesn't look tidy' — Ed explains he had beers after finishing the cleaning, implying the post-clean beer session created new mess
jokes.explanation: Strongly character-specific — only Ed would celebrate cleaning by immediately re-dirtying the space. The logic is internally consistent (he did clean, then had beers) which makes it funnier than pure stupidity.

jokes.text: Ed's messages: 'Your mum rang about tomorrow night. Liz rang about eating out. Then your mum rang back to see if I wanted to eat her out tonight.'
jokes.setup: Ed is relaying phone messages in sequence; the first two are mundane and accurate
jokes.punchline: The third message is a crude sexual pun replacing 'eat her out for dinner' with 'eat her out' — presented with identical deadpan delivery as the others
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The structure is flawless: two straight setups lull you into an expectation of boring messages, then the third is completely filthy but delivered with identical mundane cadence. The 'eat her out tonight' pun only lands because of the setup architecture — this is not cheap shock comedy, it's genuinely well-constructed. Ed's straight-faced delivery ('Wasn't true about your mum') adds a perfect button.

jokes.text: 'Sorry, we just gave away the last table.' — restaurant call immediately fails
jokes.setup: Shaun finally gets around to calling the restaurant, admitting 'I know it's short notice'
jokes.punchline: They gave away the last table moments before he called
jokes.explanation: Functional plot comedy — the punishment fits the procrastination. Not especially novel but efficiently delivered.

jokes.text: Ed's Winchester solution: 'They don't do food.' / 'There's a Breville out back.'
jokes.setup: Shaun needs a restaurant for a romantic anniversary dinner; Ed suggests the Winchester
jokes.punchline: When Shaun points out the Winchester doesn't do food, Ed counters that there's a toasted sandwich maker in the back — as though this solves the problem
jokes.explanation: Ed's solution being a toasted sandwich maker is perfectly absurd and perfectly him — he genuinely sees this as an adequate romantic dinner solution. 'There's a Breville out back' is quotable precisely because it's specific (a Breville, not 'a sandwich toaster') and because it's delivered as a reasonable alternative. Gets rewatch_bonus because the Winchester becomes genuinely important to the plot.

jokes.text: Liz: 'You didn't book it, did you, Shaun?' / Shaun: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Shaun has just admitted there's been a 'mix-up' with the table
jokes.punchline: Liz cuts to the truth in one question; Shaun confirms with a single flat 'No'
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy. Liz's intuition, Shaun's undisguised capitulation, and the flatness of the 'No' are all doing the work. The comedy is entirely in the gap between his elaborate fictions and the blunt truth landing in one monosyllable.

jokes.text: Shaun's answer to 'What is the plan, then?' — The Winchester
jokes.setup: Liz has just rejected the idea of the Winchester; now, with no restaurant available, Shaun is out of options
jokes.punchline: He suggests the Winchester again anyway, delivered with zero guile
jokes.explanation: The Winchester is already the punchline to multiple previous jokes. Shaun suggesting it again, completely earnestly, as his actual answer is both the perfect character moment and a callback to multiple threads simultaneously. Rewatch_bonus because the Winchester becomes the film's refuge/solution — suggesting it here is funny on rewatch for a different reason than it's funny on first viewing.

jokes.text: Shaun: 'Do you want me to climb up the wall, come through the window? Because I will.' / Dianne: 'You're not coming in.' / Shaun: 'OK, see you in a minute.'
jokes.setup: Dianne refuses to let Shaun in through the intercom because Liz doesn't want to see him
jokes.punchline: Shaun gives her a warning he'll climb in through the window; she refuses; he announces he'll be there in a minute anyway — turning the warning into a declaration
jokes.explanation: 'OK, see you in a minute' as a response to being told 'you're not coming in' is perfectly Shaun — he treats the threat as a statement of intent rather than a question. Good comedic timing baked into the script.

jokes.text: "You promised you'd stop smoking." / "You promised you'd try drinking red wine instead of beer!" / "We went to Greece!" "At a rave." / "You promised us free cable."
jokes.setup: Shaun tries to promise things will change; Liz catalogues all his broken promises
jokes.punchline: The list of promises escalates — from smoking, to wine, to holidays ('We went to Greece!' / 'At a rave.' — meaning it wasn't really a holiday), landing on the absurdly mundane 'You promised us free cable'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the standout sequences of the reel. The escalation from 'smoking' (personal health) to 'red wine instead of beer' (lifestyle) to 'holiday' — defeated by 'at a rave' — to 'free cable' (the pettiest possible broken promise) is pitch-perfect. 'At a rave' as a one-line demolition of Shaun's claim to have taken Liz on holiday is excellent economy. The anticlimax of 'free cable' as the list's conclusion is absurdist and very funny. Earns 8+ because every beat is deliberate and the structure is impeccable.

jokes.text: Shaun: 'That's harsh. I did not call Dianne a failed actress.'
jokes.setup: Liz quotes back Shaun calling David 'a twat' and Dianne 'a failed actress'
jokes.punchline: Shaun's only objection is to the word 'failed' — implying he might have called her an actress, just not a *failed* one (which may or may not be better)
jokes.explanation: The specific objection — not to the entire characterisation but only to the word 'failed' — implies Shaun has been precise in his insults. The ambiguity of whether he was defending Dianne's acting career or just splitting hairs is exactly the right level of comic specificity.

jokes.text: Promise inventory: smoking, red wine, holiday, free cable — Shaun: 'I'm working on that.'
jokes.setup: Liz starts listing all the promises Shaun has broken in the relationship
jokes.punchline: The list keeps escalating — smoking, wine, Greece, and then the absurd 'free cable' which Shaun is 'working on' — suggesting he has promised his girlfriend stolen cable television
jokes.explanation: The escalation from real relationship grievances to 'free cable' is perfectly pitched — it's unexpected enough to be funny while still being completely plausible for Shaun as a character. 'I'm working on that' as his response to the cable specifically (not the holiday, not the smoking) is a great character choice.

jokes.text: Shaun: 'I can give up smoking whenever I want. See, don't need them.' — immediately loses the thread
jokes.setup: Liz includes smoking in her list of broken promises
jokes.punchline: Shaun dramatically quits on the spot as proof... then immediately forgets about it and asks 'What was the next one?' as if the gesture was entirely for show
jokes.explanation: The 'see, don't need them' physical gesture followed by the immediate total forgetting of the gesture is good character comedy. His attention immediately snapping back to the list ('What was the next one?') is funnier than any remark about smoking could be.

jokes.text: David's flatmate: 'I'd say your nine lives were up, Shaun.' / Shaun: 'Get fucked, four-eyes!'
jokes.setup: David makes a pointed observation about Shaun's situation with Liz
jokes.punchline: Shaun's brilliant comeback is 'Get fucked, four-eyes' — a schoolyard insult aimed at a grown adult's glasses
jokes.explanation: 'Get fucked, four-eyes' is funny because it's a 10-year-old's insult in an adult situation. Shaun can't rebut the substance of David's point so he attacks the man's spectacles. Character-specific: Shaun's emotional maturity maxing out at playground level.

jokes.text: David (Liz's flatmate): 'You go out with her, you love her so much.' / Shaun: 'What do you mean by that?' / David: 'What do you mean by that?' / Shaun: 'I don't know what he meant by that.'
jokes.setup: David makes a loaded comment implying his own feelings for Liz
jokes.punchline: Neither Shaun nor David can fully articulate what it means; Shaun's bewildered 'I don't know what he meant by that' hangs in the air
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the awkwardness — both men avoiding what the comment clearly implies. Shaun's shrugging 'I don't know what he meant' as a final note is a good deflation that also reveals something about his emotional avoidance. Rewatch_bonus because David's feelings for Liz pay off later in the film.

jokes.text: Shaun gives Liz the 'wonderful mum' flowers — 'I thought it would be funny because of what you said last night about you don't want to be my mum'
jokes.setup: Shaun shows up to Liz's flat as a grand gesture; Liz sarcastically noted she was 'beginning to sound like his mum' the night before; Shaun bought flowers saying they were for his actual mum
jokes.punchline: He gives Liz the flowers intended for his mum — the ones labelled 'To a wonderful Mum' — and explains his reasoning with complete earnestness, calling it 'a little joke, just sort of spur of the moment'
jokes.explanation: One of the best callback jokes in the reel and in the film. It calls back to three separate setups: Liz's mum comment, Shaun buying mum flowers while being watched by Noel, and Philip's reminder. The joke is that Shaun thinks this is CHARMING — a 'little joke' — and his explanation only makes it worse. 'Just sort of spur of the moment' over a gift he laboured to purchase is perfect character comedy. Liz's flat 'They're for your mum, aren't they?' followed by 'Smooth' captures the total failure without overplaying it. Near-exceptional — the callback architecture spanning 15 minutes of film is exactly what Edgar Wright built this screenplay to do.

jokes.text: Shaun in the pub, philosophising: 'If I don't do something, I'll end up in that pub for the rest of my life like those other sad old fuckers wondering what the hell happened.' — delivered while sitting in the pub
jokes.setup: Shaun is lamenting his stagnant life and fear of ending up stuck
jokes.punchline: He delivers this speech from inside the Winchester pub, apparently without noticing the irony
jokes.explanation: The situational irony is rich — Shaun's self-awareness speech is entirely undone by his physical location. The fact that Ed doesn't point it out (he's moved on to consolation mode) makes it funnier. Rewatch_bonus as the Winchester becomes genuinely important and Shaun does, temporarily, become one of those people.

jokes.text: Ed's post-breakup consolation: 'Fuck her. You got your pint. You got your pig snacks. What more do you want?'
jokes.setup: Shaun is heartbroken after being dumped; Ed is trying to help
jokes.punchline: Ed's entire philosophy of life — pint plus pig snacks — is offered as a genuine and complete answer to existential grief
jokes.explanation: Ed's worldview distilled to its essence: a pint and pig snacks are sufficient comfort for any human suffering. The specificity of 'pig snacks' (not crisps, not pork scratchings — pig snacks) is the extra detail that makes it quotable. High character integration because this is 100% Ed's philosophy and nobody else's.

jokes.text: Ed: 'Oh. You want your favourite monkey? Shall I do Clyde?' — followed by a full orang-utan impression to cheer up the heartbroken Shaun
jokes.setup: Ed is trying increasingly desperate measures to cheer Shaun up; established earlier that he can do an orang-utan impression
jokes.punchline: He calls it 'Clyde' — giving the impression a name and favourite status — and apparently performs it at length enough to genuinely cheer Shaun up
jokes.explanation: The callback to Pete's dismissive orang-utan jab is now recontextualised as Ed's most heartfelt act of friendship — the same thing Pete mocked is the thing that actually works. Naming it 'Clyde' and treating it as Shaun's 'favourite' gives the impression an emotional history. The payoff (Shaun actually cheers up) validates the whole Ed-as-friend argument the film has been making. Earns 8.0 because the callback structure rewards patient viewers.

jokes.text: "See, I knew you'd get over her." — Ed, immediately after the orang-utan impression, taking Shaun's laugh as proof of recovery
jokes.setup: Shaun laughs involuntarily at Ed's impression
jokes.punchline: Ed immediately misreads this as Shaun being completely over Liz — the impression has 'cured' him, in Ed's view
jokes.explanation: Ed's confident psychological assessment is funny because it's completely wrong but totally sincere. 'See, I knew you'd get over her' delivered as if the case is closed is perfect Ed — he has zero emotional sophistication but maximum confidence. Good character economy.

jokes.text: "If You Leave Me Now" plays on the jukebox on random — Shaun: 'Who the hell put this on?' / Ed: 'It's on random.'
jokes.setup: Shaun is freshly dumped and sitting in the pub
jokes.punchline: The jukebox selects the most on-the-nose possible breakup song at random
jokes.explanation: The 'universe conspires against the sad character' jukebox joke is a familiar device but 'It's on random' as a defensive answer is a good straight-man delivery. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Ed's plan for tomorrow: 'A Bloody Mary first thing, a bite at the King's Head, couple at The Little Princess, stagger back here and bang... back at the bar for shots. How's that for a slice of fried gold?'
jokes.setup: Shaun is heartbroken; Ed is offering a recovery plan
jokes.punchline: Ed's entire plan is a full pub crawl with zero non-drinking activities, presented with enormous pride and the phrase 'slice of fried gold' as its self-congratulatory kicker
jokes.explanation: 'How's that for a slice of fried gold?' is one of the film's most quotable phrases — it's Ed presenting a pub crawl as a masterwork of planning. The specificity of the pub names and the trajectory ('stagger back here') gives it the feeling of a genuine itinerary, which is funnier than a vague suggestion. High quotability.

jokes.text: Ed's pub regulars: 'These are rich, interesting characters.' / 'Like who?' — building invented biographies for a bigamist, a porn star, and a mafia man
jokes.setup: Shaun repeats Liz's criticism that the pub regulars are 'sad old fuckers'; Ed defends them
jokes.punchline: Ed's defence is a series of elaborately invented criminal/salacious biographies: a bigamist who invented the mobile disco, an ex-porn star, and a North London mafia barman — all delivered as fact
jokes.explanation: One of the best comedic sequences in the reel. Each biography is funnier than the last: the bigamist detail 'strangled his first wife with a draught excluder and invented the mobile disco' is a brilliantly specific non-sequitur pairing. 'Cockacidal maniac' as a descriptor is a genuinely inventive coinage. 'Cafe Au Lait Pour Vous' as a porn film title is absurdist precision comedy. The sequence earns 8.0 for sustained originality and escalating comic invention.

jokes.text: "Ooh! Cockacidal maniac." "She's an ex-porn star. They say she starred in the world's first interracial hardcore loop. Cafe Au Lait Pour Vous."
jokes.setup: Ed continues with another pub regular, an older woman
jokes.punchline: 'Cockacidal maniac' as an invented portmanteau, followed by the escalating porn-film backstory, capped by the genuinely funny fake French title 'Cafe Au Lait Pour Vous'
jokes.explanation: 'Cockacidal maniac' is an invented word that earns its laughs — it's specific, outrageous, and Ed-plausible. The fake French film title 'Cafe Au Lait Pour Vous' is a terrific absurdist detail: it sounds exactly like what someone who doesn't know French would construct for a film title they half-remember. High originality because the word invention is sharp.

jokes.text: "He's North London Mafia. It's true, Big Al says so." "Yeah, Big Al also says dogs can't look up."
jokes.setup: Ed claims John the barman is 'North London Mafia,' citing Big Al as a source
jokes.punchline: Shaun undermines the credibility of Big Al's intelligence by citing another of his theories: 'dogs can't look up'
jokes.explanation: One of the most famous lines in the film. 'Dogs can't look up' is a perfectly chosen absurd piece of misinformation — it's specific, testable, and completely wrong, which makes Big Al's credibility collapse hilariously. The structure (source cited → source discredited via equally absurd claim) is impeccable. Maximum economy — Shaun's rebuttal is nine words. Earns 8.5+ because the specific choice of 'dogs can't look up' is genuinely inspired; any other claim would have been less funny.

jokes.text: 'Why is there a rifle above the bar?' / 'The pub's called the Winchester.' / 'Exactly.'
jokes.setup: Ed is building the case that the barman John is North London Mafia; evidence includes a rifle above the bar
jokes.punchline: Shaun points out it's because the pub is called the Winchester; Ed treats this as confirmation rather than refutation
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat joke. Shaun's mundane explanation (the name of the pub) is precisely the right answer, but Ed's 'Exactly' treats it as evidence in his favour — implying the pub was possibly *named* the Winchester because of the rifle/mafia connection. The word 'Exactly' is doing all the work and it's a single syllable. Gets rewatch_bonus because the Winchester rifle becomes genuinely important to the film's resolution. One of the most elegant jokes in the reel.

jokes.text: Ed's speech: 'I'm not gonna say there's plenty more fish in the sea, I'm not gonna say if you love her let her go...' — building to 'it's not the end of the world'
jokes.setup: Ed promises not to use clichés to comfort Shaun, listing several he's explicitly not going to use
jokes.punchline: 'It's not the end of the world' — which is itself a cliché, delivered as though it's something profound he arrived at independently; also works as literal foreshadowing of the zombie apocalypse
jokes.explanation: Smart structure: the meta-promise not to use clichés, followed by a cliché, is a solid joke on its own. The rewatch_bonus earns its keep here because 'it's not the end of the world' is literally wrong — by the film's end, the world (as they know it) has ended. This is Edgar Wright planting a thematic joke that only pays off across the whole film.

jokes.text: A woman staggers to the pub door; Shaun tells her 'Sorry, we're closed' and then dismisses her as a 'pisshead'
jokes.setup: A person is stumbling toward the pub; Shaun and Ed are inside
jokes.punchline: Shaun dismisses what is almost certainly an early zombie as a drunk — 'Pisshead' — perfectly capturing the film's central joke of the mundane masking the apocalyptic
jokes.explanation: One of the most tonally perfect jokes in the reel. The 'pisshead' dismissal of a zombie is both funny as a character joke (Shaun's obliviousness) and structurally important (setting up how normal people miss the zombie outbreak). Gets rewatch_bonus heavily — on second viewing, the horror of this moment sits alongside the comedy, which is exactly what the film is built to do.

jokes.text: Ed and Shaun playing 'White Lines' and dancing/acting out the song in the pub at night, using the record as a prop while everyone around them has gone
jokes.setup: It's late; the pub is empty; Ed and Shaun are drunk and alone
jokes.punchline: They enact an elaborate lip-sync/air guitar/instruction-following of the Grandmaster Flash song, including 'Blow!' and debating whether the rapper should say 'base' or 'freeze'
jokes.explanation: The charm of this sequence is entirely in the commitment — two grown men earnestly analysing whether the rapper 'should say base or freeze' while performing to an empty pub. 'What a tit' as the closing judgment on the rapper is a good button. Character-specific: this is what Shaun and Ed actually do instead of growing up.

jokes.text: Pete's expletive explosion: 'It's fucking Sunday and I've got to go to fucking work in four fucking hours because every other fucker is fucking ill!'
jokes.setup: Shaun tries to deflect Pete's anger with 'It's Saturday' (it's not)
jokes.punchline: Pete's correction is a spectacular f-bomb escalation cataloguing his exact grievances — four uses of 'fucking' in one sentence — capped with 'Now can you see why I'm so fucking angry?'
jokes.explanation: The f-bomb count in that sentence is itself the joke — Pete's rage expressed through sheer density of profanity, then punctuated with the rhetorical 'Now can you see why?' as though he's made a logical argument. The structure (grievance + rhetorical validation request) is very specific to the character's wound-up professional type.

jokes.text: Shaun: 'I'm sorry, we had a couple of drinks, we split up with Liz tonight.' — first-person plural on the breakup
jokes.setup: Shaun is apologising to Pete for the noise
jokes.punchline: 'We split up with Liz' — Shaun uses 'we' as though Ed was also in the relationship, treating Ed's involvement in the breakup as equivalent to his own
jokes.explanation: 'We split up with Liz' is a small but very precise character joke — Shaun and Ed as an indivisible social unit. The 'we' unintentionally confirms everything Pete and Liz have been saying about Ed's centrality to Shaun's life. Great economy.

jokes.text: Ed mutters 'Prick' at Pete under his breath; Pete hears; confrontation begins — 'What was that?' / 'Nothing.' / 'Stop it, we're friends!'
jokes.setup: Pete has just stormed back upstairs; Ed mutters the insult thinking he's out of earshot
jokes.punchline: Pete hears it perfectly; Ed's 'Nothing' is transparently false; Shaun's 'Stop it, we're friends!' is an absurd diplomatic appeal
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom escalation beat — the whispered insult that's heard — but 'Stop it, we're friends!' from Shaun is a funny addition because it insists on a social harmony that clearly does not exist between Pete and Ed.

jokes.text: Pete: 'All he ever does is hold you back. Or is it easier having someone around who's more of a loser than you?'
jokes.setup: Pete is in full righteous-anger mode about Ed
jokes.punchline: He pivots from attacking Ed to attacking Shaun with 'or is it easier having someone around who's more of a loser than you?' — a genuinely cutting observation that hits differently than a typical insult
jokes.explanation: Pete's insight is genuinely perceptive and uncomfortable — which makes it funny in a dark-subversive way. The joke is that Pete, in a fit of furious rudeness, says the truest thing anyone has said in the entire reel. Rewatch_bonus because the film ultimately validates Pete's theory.

jokes.text: Pete: 'I assume it was Liz who did the dumping?' — cool factual interrogation mid-argument
jokes.setup: Pete is mid-rant about Shaun's life choices
jokes.punchline: He pauses to coolly verify his assumption about who dumped whom — treating the emotional revelation as an administrative fact to be confirmed before proceeding
jokes.explanation: The deadpan aside in the middle of a lecture is a great structural beat. Pete's 'I assume' treats the humiliating truth as so obvious it barely needs confirming — which is itself a form of contempt that's funnier than any direct insult.

jokes.text: Pete: 'Sort your fucking life out, mate.' — and then immediately: 'What's up with your hand?'
jokes.setup: Pete delivers his devastating life-assessment and seems about to storm off
jokes.punchline: He immediately notices Ed's injured/bitten hand and pivots to genuine concern — the tonal whiplash from savage to practical is the joke
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'sort your life out' to 'what's up with your hand' is a sharp tonal reversal. Gets rewatch_bonus because Pete's bitten hand becomes a major plot point — the audience laughs at Pete demanding normalcy while already being infected.

jokes.text: Pete: bitten by 'crackheads' on the way home / 'Why did they bite you?' / 'I don't know, I didn't stop to ask them!'
jokes.setup: Pete reveals he was mugged and bitten by people he describes as crackheads
jokes.punchline: Ed's question 'Why did they bite you?' is treated as imbecilic by Pete; his frustrated 'I didn't stop to ask them!' is both a reasonable response and a darkly ironic joke given that the biters were zombies
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes of the reel on rewatch — Pete has been bitten by a zombie and nobody knows it. 'Why did they bite you?' is simultaneously a dumb question and the most important question in the scene. 'I didn't stop to ask them' is exactly the right response from someone who doesn't know they've just been given a death sentence. The dark irony layers perfectly with the horror premise without tipping the film's hand.

jokes.text: Ed: 'It's not hip hop, it's electro. Prick.'
jokes.setup: Pete objects to Shaun and Ed's late-night music ('your stupid hip hop isn't helping')
jokes.punchline: Ed's only contribution to the whole confrontation is a genre correction and a parting insult, once Pete is upstairs
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: (1) Ed staying completely silent through the entire argument and then contributing only a genre pedantry, and (2) 'Prick' delivered with quiet dignity once Pete is out of earshot. It's perfectly Ed — he can't engage with the substance of Pete's points but he can correct the music taxonomy. High character integration and economy: eight words, two laughs.

jokes.text: Ed: 'Next time I see him, he's dead.' — said about Pete, who will shortly actually be undead
jokes.setup: Ed is furious at Pete after the confrontation
jokes.punchline: 'He's dead' as a figure of speech — except Pete is in the process of turning into a zombie, making Ed accidentally prophetic
jokes.explanation: One of the purest instances of Edgar Wright's foreshadowing-as-punchline technique. 'He's dead' is a throwaway angry figure of speech that becomes literally true in a horror-comedy sense. The joke has two completely different meanings — one on first viewing, one on rewatch — and both work. High quotability.

jokes.text: Mum's voicemail coda: 'Cos these days a lot of people don't eat meat.'
jokes.setup: Mum is asking if Liz wants anything special for lunch, mid-anxious-hostess mode
jokes.punchline: Her closing concern is the possibility that Liz might be vegetarian — a sweet, hilariously practical domestic worry that deflates all the drama
jokes.explanation: The reel ends on this detail — a sweet, completely ordinary motherly concern about vegetarianism immediately after a zombie-bite, a breakup, a confrontation, and Pete's profane meltdown. The tonal contrast is itself the joke. 'These days a lot of people don't eat meat' as the closing line of a reel building toward a zombie film is a perfect, low-key button.

jokes.text: Shaun asks Ed if he wants anything from the shop; Ed says simply 'Cornetto.'
jokes.setup: The world is apparently falling apart — there are eerie, unacknowledged signs of zombie activity all around — and Shaun casually asks if Ed wants anything from the corner shop.
jokes.punchline: Ed's only request is a Cornetto ice cream, treating the apocalypse with total indifference.
jokes.explanation: This is the film's title joke — 'Cornetto' becomes the comedic thesis of the entire Cornetto trilogy. The economy is flawless: one word, delivered deadpan, against the backdrop of imminent catastrophe. The character integration is extraordinary because only Ed, whose appetite and laziness are his defining traits, could reduce the zombie apocalypse to an ice cream order. It earns 9+ on craft because it functions simultaneously as a plot beat, a character joke, a running gag seed, and a cultural artifact. It's among the best single-word punchlines in British comedy cinema.

jokes.text: Shaun tries to buy a paper from the newsagent Nelson, admits 'I owe you about 15p' and can't pay — while zombie chaos is unfolding around him.
jokes.setup: Shaun walks through streets beginning to show signs of zombie activity, oblivious, and tries to do mundane corner-shop transactions.
jokes.punchline: His biggest problem is that he's 15p short for a newspaper — the mundane financial embarrassment dwarfs the apocalypse for him.
jokes.explanation: Classic Wright/Pegg obliviousness comedy — the horror of the world registers zero while petty social embarrassment dominates. The 15p detail is brilliantly specific and very British. Works best on rewatch when you know exactly what Shaun is NOT noticing.

jokes.text: 'Oh dear.' — Shaun's reaction, twice, to something alarming in the shop (presumably a zombie or aftermath), delivered in the most understated British manner possible.
jokes.setup: Shaun is in the shop, notices something deeply wrong.
jokes.punchline: His only response is a soft, polite 'Oh dear' — the most inadequate possible reaction to zombie horror.
jokes.explanation: Two words carrying enormous comedic weight. Pegg's performance of quintessential British understatement in the face of the apocalypse is exactly the film's comic engine. The economy score is near-perfect — 'oh dear' is the most compressed possible version of this joke.

jokes.text: The TV/radio channels briefly sync up: zombie attack news reports are intercut with a pop song ('Panic' by The Smiths) and a pop chart show, accidentally forming coherent sentences.
jokes.setup: Multiple media sources broadcasting simultaneously about the zombie crisis.
jokes.punchline: The channels accidentally stitch together the sentence 'people who are being... eaten alive' and the chart-topper line interrupts mid-report — the trivial and the horrific collide in one broadcast montage.
jokes.explanation: Edgar Wright's directorial wit at its sharpest — the editing joke where channel-flipping accidentally assembles horror context from pop culture noise. Genuinely original structural comedy that works on the page but truly fires in execution. Character integration is low because it's a directorial/structural joke rather than a character joke.

jokes.text: 'She's so drunk.' — Shaun and Ed's diagnosis of the zombie girl stumbling in the garden.
jokes.setup: A clearly zombified girl is lurching terrifyingly in the garden — pale, stiff, groaning.
jokes.punchline: Their first assumption is that she's simply very drunk, normalising the supernatural into the mundane.
jokes.explanation: Perfect encapsulation of the film's central comic premise: Shaun and Ed are so embedded in their lad pub culture that zombie behaviour reads as extreme drunkenness. The character integration is excellent — only these specific young men, used to seeing people in this state on a Friday, would reach this conclusion first.

jokes.text: 'How much have you had, love?' / 'Oh! I think she likes you.' / 'She wants a cuddle!' / 'I've just come out of a relationship.'
jokes.setup: The zombie girl is approaching Shaun menacingly.
jokes.punchline: Ed jokes that the zombie fancies Shaun; Shaun deflects with the deadpan 'I've just come out of a relationship' — treating undead assault as an unwanted romantic advance.
jokes.explanation: A three-beat escalating exchange where Ed's lad banter meets Shaun's obliviousness. Shaun's 'I've just come out of a relationship' is the standout — it treats zombie peril as social awkwardness, which is both funny and quietly reveals his emotional state. The quotability is high because the line travels well out of context.

jokes.text: 'Mary, I'm warning you, I'll have to get physical, I mean it!'
jokes.setup: Shaun is being attacked by a zombie and treating it like a social negotiation he wants to avoid escalating.
jokes.punchline: He issues a formal warning to the zombie, as if she's a rowdy pub patron he's reluctant to manhandle — complete politeness under existential threat.
jokes.explanation: Shaun's conflict-averse, polite British nature rendered absurd by zombie context. The specificity of calling her 'Mary' and the formal warning structure ('I'm warning you...I mean it') is excellent character writing.

jokes.text: 'How about an ambulance?' / 'It's engaged, Ed.' / 'Fire engine?' / 'It's one number and it's busy!' / 'And what do you want a fire engine for?' / 'Anything with flashing lights.'
jokes.setup: Emergency services are unreachable during the zombie crisis. Shaun is frantically trying 999.
jokes.punchline: Ed's suggestions escalate from sensible (ambulance) to useless (fire engine), justified by 'anything with flashing lights' — revealing his child-like panic logic.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best pure dialogue jokes. The escalation is perfectly structured: ambulance (logical) → fire engine (illogical) → 'anything with flashing lights' (pure childlike id). That final punchline is a genuine character revelation — Ed's panic strips him to pure toddler instinct. High quotability. The structure score reflects how cleanly the three-beat exchange builds and pays off.

jokes.text: 'What do you think we should do?' / 'Have a sit-down?'
jokes.setup: Zombies are surrounding the house; chaos on the news. Shaun asks what they should do.
jokes.punchline: Ed's suggestion is 'have a sit-down' — the laziest, most passive response to an active apocalypse.
jokes.explanation: Very economical character joke — Ed's defining trait (laziness) expressed in three words. Not as sharp as 'anything with flashing lights' but efficient.

jokes.text: 'We can take 'em.' / 'The man said to stay indoors.' / 'Fuck the man.' / 'In here, we're safe.' — the debate about going outside.
jokes.setup: The TV has just told them to stay indoors. Ed wants to go fight zombies.
jokes.punchline: Ed's alpha-male posturing ('We can take 'em') against Shaun's anxious rule-following ('The man said to stay indoors') — two equally useless approaches to survival.
jokes.explanation: Solid character dynamic joke — Ed's bravado vs. Shaun's compliance. 'Fuck the man' from someone whose survival plan is 'sit down' is a nice internal contradiction.

jokes.text: 'Aim for the head.' — Shaun, after the TV news has just told them to destroy the brain.
jokes.setup: The TV has just announced the method to neutralise zombies: 'removing the head or destroying the brain.'
jokes.punchline: Shaun repeats this back as if it's his own tactical insight, with no acknowledgement that he just heard it on TV.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed callback — the news tells them the answer, there's a brief beat, then Shaun confidently delivers it as his own strategy. The gap between the TV announcement and Shaun's 'tactical' delivery is the joke. Very economical.

jokes.text: 'No! That's the second album I ever bought!' — Shaun's protest as Ed throws his vinyl records at zombies.
jokes.setup: Shaun and Ed need weapons to throw at zombies in the garden; they grab his record collection.
jokes.punchline: Shaun's horror is about losing a beloved record, not about the zombie apocalypse — his sentimental attachment to music outweighs his survival instincts.
jokes.explanation: The record-throwing sequence is a gem of character comedy. Shaun's most visceral emotional reaction in the whole zombie encounter is about his second album — deeply revealing of his arrested-development man-child character. Sets up the brilliant record-vetting sequence that follows.

jokes.text: The record vetting sequence: Ed proposes records to throw; Shaun adjudicates each ('Purple Rain?' / 'No.' / 'Sign O' The Times?' / 'Definitely not.' / 'The Batman soundtrack?' / 'Throw it.' / 'Dire Straits?' / 'Throw it.' / 'Stone Roses?' / 'No.' / 'Second Coming?' / 'I like it.' / 'Sade?' / 'That's Liz's.' / 'She dumped you.')
jokes.setup: They need ammunition; Shaun must decide which records are expendable. Each record is a micro-verdict on taste, sentimentality, and his ex-girlfriend.
jokes.punchline: The sequence escalates beautifully: Prince is sacred; The Batman soundtrack and Dire Straits are disposable without hesitation; Second Coming gets a sentimental defence; Sade belongs to Liz, so Ed notes 'she dumped you' — using the apocalypse to relitigate the breakup.
jokes.explanation: Among the best sustained comedic sequences in the film and arguably the best in this reel. It works on multiple levels simultaneously: (1) it's a genuinely funny rapid-fire escalation, (2) each record choice is a character revelation (Prince is non-negotiable; Batman soundtrack is trash), (3) the Liz callback lands perfectly — Ed weaponising the breakup mid-zombie-fight — and (4) the mundane life-or-death stakes inversion is pitch-perfect. The structure is impeccable: eight micro-beats, each with its own punchline, building to the emotional kicker at the end. Comparable in quality to the vasectomy escalation anchor provided.

jokes.text: 'You've got red on you.' — said to Shaun after he's been in zombie combat, blood-spattered.
jokes.setup: In Reel 1, this phrase was used in a mundane context (ketchup, paint, etc.). Here Shaun has real blood/zombie matter on him.
jokes.punchline: The same phrase, repeated in a horrifically literal context, landing with fresh absurdity because the speaker still treats it as a minor social observation.
jokes.explanation: The film's most elegant running gag. The phrase's transformation from mundane social nicety to genuine blood-spatter observation, delivered with identical casual affect, is a masterclass in callback comedy. The economy is perfect — four words carry enormous structural weight. Earns 8.5+ because it's genuinely surprising on first watch and deeply satisfying on rewatch.

jokes.text: The debate about going upstairs to check on Pete: 'Because A, he might be one of them and B, he might still be annoyed.' — Shaun's two-reason list treating zombie transformation and social awkwardness as equal dangers.
jokes.setup: They're debating whether to check on flatmate Pete, who was bitten and is upstairs.
jokes.punchline: Shaun lists 'he might be a zombie' and 'he might be annoyed at us' as parallel dangers of equal weight.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely exceptional joke. The A/B structure gives it the feel of a formal risk assessment, and the bathos of equating undead danger with social awkwardness is perfectly calibrated. 'He might still be annoyed' as a reason not to check on a potential zombie is as good a character joke as the film has. High quotability.

jokes.text: 'Oi, prick! He's not in.' — Ed shouts up at Pete's room and concludes he's absent.
jokes.setup: They're trying to establish whether Pete is upstairs and potentially dangerous. Ed's method of investigation is to shout an insult at him.
jokes.punchline: Ed's chosen greeting to a potentially zombified housemate is 'Oi, prick!' — and the lack of response is conclusive evidence that 'He's not in.'
jokes.explanation: Pure Ed — his social register doesn't change whether the stakes are low or apocalyptically high. Calling Pete 'prick' as a neutral greeting and treating no response as evidence of absence (rather than incapacitation) is both very funny and completely on-brand.

jokes.text: 'Maybe he went into work.' / 'How come he didn't drive? His keys are still here.' / 'Maybe he got a lift. He said he wasn't feeling well.'
jokes.setup: Pete has almost certainly become a zombie. The keys are still there. The signs are obvious.
jokes.punchline: They construct an elaborate mundane explanation (he got a lift to work despite being ill) rather than accept the obvious zombie conclusion.
jokes.explanation: More of the film's core obliviousness comedy — the characters constructing normal-world explanations for obviously supernatural events. Competent but not as sharp as the similar beats elsewhere.

jokes.text: 'Well... they were a bit bitey.' — Barbara's description of zombie attackers.
jokes.setup: Shaun is urgently asking his mum if she's OK, whether the men who tried to break in hurt her.
jokes.punchline: Barbara's characterisation of zombie attackers as merely 'a bit bitey' — as if describing slightly over-enthusiastic dogs — is the ultimate British understatement of mortal peril.
jokes.explanation: One of the film's finest single-line jokes and among the best in this reel. 'A bit bitey' is as perfect a piece of British understatement as has ever been written for screen. It's 100% character-specific — only a certain type of English mum would describe a zombie swarm this way. The economy is flawless. Comparable to the 'Oh dear' register but far more original and specific. This is a quotability 9.5 — it's become genuinely iconic.

jokes.text: 'No, but Philip has.' / 'Oh, OK.' (beat) / 'Oh, OK.' — The relay of Philip's zombie bite delivered and received with eerie calm.
jokes.setup: Shaun asks if his mum has been bitten. She says no, but Philip has.
jokes.punchline: Both Shaun and Ed receive the news of Philip's zombie bite with 'Oh, OK' — as if told he has a mild cold. The double 'Oh, OK' (once from each) plays as a deadpan relay of catastrophic information.
jokes.explanation: The doubled 'Oh, OK' is a lovely structural beat — the information is passed like a mundane relay message, the horror completely evacuated by delivery. Works best in performance.

jokes.text: 'We may have to kill my stepdad.'
jokes.setup: Philip has been bitten; Shaun absorbs the information.
jokes.punchline: Shaun's calm, matter-of-fact conclusion — 'we may have to kill my stepdad' — delivered as casually as a shopping list item, with a hedge word 'may' doing enormous comedic work.
jokes.explanation: The 'may' is doing all the heavy lifting — the hedging word transforms patricide-adjacent planning into polite tentativeness. Character-perfect for Shaun, who can't commit to anything decisively. Also darkly funny because it's genuinely the right conclusion. High quotability — this line is frequently cited.

jokes.text: 'We're coming to get you, Barbara!' — Shaun's declaration, echoing the famous Night of the Living Dead line.
jokes.setup: Shaun tells his mum they're coming to rescue her.
jokes.punchline: The phrasing directly quotes the iconic line from Night of the Living Dead ('They're coming to get you, Barbara!') — a meta zombie-movie reference embedded in a sincere moment.
jokes.explanation: A genre-aware gag that works on two levels: sincere rescue call and horror movie homage. The fact that his mum is actually named Barbara makes it perfect. Earns rewatch bonus because genre-literate audiences catch it immediately while others just get the sincere version.

jokes.text: Shaun's plan monologue: 'We take Pete's car, we drive over to Mum's, we go in, we take care of Philip... then we grab Mum, go over to Liz's place, hole up, have a cup of tea and wait for all this to blow over.'
jokes.setup: Zombie apocalypse is in full swing. Shaun is formulating a survival plan.
jokes.punchline: The plan climaxes with 'have a cup of tea and wait for all this to blow over' — the most quintessentially English solution to the end of the world.
jokes.explanation: The plan is both funny as written and sets up the running gag as it gets refined over three iterations. 'Have a cup of tea and wait for all this to blow over' is a defining cultural joke — the British response to any crisis. The plan's repeated refinements add escalating comedy.

jokes.text: 'Why have we got to go to Liz's?' / 'Because we do.' / 'She dumped you.' / 'I have to know if she's all right.' / 'Why?' / 'Because I love her.' / 'All right, gay.'
jokes.setup: Shaun insists on rescuing Liz as part of the plan. Ed challenges him.
jokes.punchline: Ed's response to Shaun's sincere romantic declaration ('Because I love her') is 'All right, gay' — aggressively anti-sentimental, perfectly in character.
jokes.explanation: Ed's reflex homophobia as emotional-deflection comedy — a very British male response to sincerity. The word lands as character comedy rather than gratuitous slur because it so precisely captures Ed's refusal to process emotions. The timing is impeccable.

jokes.text: Ed's conditions for holing up: 'If we hole up, I want to be somewhere familiar, I wanna know where the exits are and I wanna be allowed to smoke.'
jokes.setup: They're debating where to shelter during the zombie apocalypse. Ed has tactical objections.
jokes.punchline: Ed's survival criteria prioritise smoking rights above all strategic concerns — his list sounds tactical but bottoms out at 'allowed to smoke.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ed character joke — his three criteria parody genuine tactical thinking, then collapse into petty self-interest. The build from 'familiar' to 'know the exits' makes it sound like a real survivalist, then 'allowed to smoke' deflates it. Character integration is 9 because this is Ed's personality condensed.

jokes.text: Ed's conditions repeated as the location shifts: 'Where can I smoke?' — now it's the only criterion that matters.
jokes.setup: Shaun is asking what makes an ideal location ('where's safe? where's familiar?').
jokes.punchline: Ed has already reduced the entire survival criteria to 'where can I smoke?' — the question now asked alone, stripped of the other pretences.
jokes.explanation: The running gag stripped to its essence — four words now doing what a whole list did moments ago. Classic comedic compression.

jokes.text: The Winchester plan: 'Take car, go to Mum's, kill Phil. Sorry. Grab Liz, go to the Winchester, have a nice cold pint and wait for all this to blow over.'
jokes.setup: The plan has been iterated twice. This is the third and final version, landing on the pub as the logical safe house.
jokes.punchline: The plan culminates in 'go to the Winchester, have a nice cold pint and wait for all this to blow over' — the pub as zombie apocalypse solution, fulfilling the film's premise. 'Kill Phil. Sorry.' is a perfectly placed dark beat.
jokes.explanation: This is the film's thesis statement as punchline — the entire premise of 'Shaun of the Dead' (pub as apocalypse solution) crystallised in one perfectly structured plan. The three-iteration build is textbook comedic escalation, with the Winchester landing as both the logical and absurd conclusion. 'Kill Phil. Sorry.' mid-plan is a beautiful dark aside. Among the most quotable lines in British comedy cinema.

jokes.text: Final plan: 'Take car, go to Mum's, kill Phil. Sorry. Grab Liz, go to the Winchester, have a nice cold pint and wait for all this to blow over.'
jokes.setup: Third and final version of the plan. Shaun now resolves the destination question.
jokes.punchline: The Winchester replaces Liz's flat as the sanctuary — the local pub where Shaun proposed a pint at the start of the film. 'Have a nice cold pint' as a zombie apocalypse survival strategy is the culmination of the film's thesis.
jokes.explanation: The most quotable line in the film and the payload of the entire three-plan running gag. The Winchester callback completes the film's central comic argument: that British pub culture is a valid response to any crisis. 'Have a nice cold pint and wait for all this to blow over' has become a cultural shorthand. The structure — building through three plan revisions to this single perfect destination — is impeccable screenwriting. This is the film's most iconic comedic moment.

jokes.text: 'How's that for a slice of fried gold?'
jokes.setup: Shaun has just delivered the Winchester plan.
jokes.punchline: He self-congratulates with 'how's that for a slice of fried gold?' — callback to Reel 1 slang while also being an absurd piece of self-satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: Callback to established character slang that now lands with more colour because we know Shaun. His self-satisfaction is endearing and absurd given the circumstances.

jokes.text: 'Do you believe everything you hear on TV?' — Shaun, dismissing the advice to stay home, preparing to leave.
jokes.setup: The TV has just told them to stay home and avoid all contact. Shaun is about to do the opposite.
jokes.punchline: He dismisses the TV advice with sceptic rhetoric — immediately after the same TV just told him how to kill zombies, which he absorbed and repeated as his own idea.
jokes.explanation: Nice irony — the man who just parroted the TV's zombie-killing advice is now dismissing its survival guidance. Works best on rewatch.

jokes.text: The 'Z word' exchange: 'Any zombies out there?' / 'Don't say that.' / 'What?' / 'That.' / 'What?' / 'That. The Z word. Don't say it.' / 'Why not?' / 'Because it's ridiculous.' / 'All right. Are there any out there, though?'
jokes.setup: Ed asks about zombies; Shaun objects to the word.
jokes.punchline: Shaun refuses to say 'zombie' because it's 'ridiculous' — a meta-commentary on the genre while also being completely sensible and completely pointless since they're literally in a zombie film. Ed's immediate re-ask without the word is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant meta-genre gag. The refusal to say 'zombie' because it's 'ridiculous' satirises both horror movie characters who refuse to name their predicament and the audience's awareness of genre. The 'That. That. That.' repetition and Ed immediately rephrasing without the word ('are there any out there, though?') shows perfect comedic timing and structure. Genuinely original.

jokes.text: 'Can't see any. Maybe it's not as bad as all that.' (beat) 'Oh! No, there they are.'
jokes.setup: Shaun looks outside to assess the zombie situation, cautiously optimistic.
jokes.punchline: Brief hope — 'maybe it's not as bad as all that' — immediately demolished by 'Oh! No, there they are.'
jokes.explanation: Classic false hope/immediate deflation structure. Well-timed and economical. Shaun's 'Oh!' of surprised discovery ('No, there they are') is a perfect anti-climax delivery.

jokes.text: 'OK, let's do this, yeah?' / 'Yeah!' / 'I got to do a wee first.'
jokes.setup: Shaun and Ed psych themselves up for zombie combat — building to a heroic moment.
jokes.punchline: The momentum of heroic resolve is immediately deflated: 'I got to do a wee first.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect bathetic timing — the heroic build-up deflated by the most mundane bodily need. Classic British anti-heroism.

jokes.text: 'OK, let's do this, yeah?' / 'Yeah!' / 'I got to do a wee first.'
jokes.setup: Shaun and Ed have a moment of action-hero resolve before heading out.
jokes.punchline: 'I got to do a wee first.' — Ed immediately deflates the moment with a mundane biological need.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation of a heroic moment. The setup (rallying cry, 'yeah!') builds expectation; 'I got to do a wee first' demolishes it immediately. The economy is excellent — it couldn't be shorter. Very Ed.

jokes.text: 'Ooh... can I drive?' / 'What?' / 'I always wanted to drive Pete's car. I might not get another chance.'
jokes.setup: They're heading out to survive the zombie apocalypse in Pete's car.
jokes.punchline: Ed's priority in this potentially final journey is not survival — it's fulfilling his dream of driving Pete's car. 'I might not get another chance' is darkly accurate and totally self-serving.
jokes.explanation: 'I might not get another chance' is doing double duty — it's both literally true (they might die) and a mundane carpe diem about a petty wish. Character integration is very high — this is entirely Ed.

jokes.text: Shaun apologises to zombie Pete for borrowing his car and invites him to the pub later: 'We'll bring it back. And if you're feeling better later, we're going to the pub. You're more than welcome to join us.'
jokes.setup: Shaun encounters Pete, now a zombie, while taking his car.
jokes.punchline: Shaun apologises to zombie Pete with full social politeness and extends a pub invitation — entirely unable to process that Pete is now undead, defaulting to British social niceties.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely exceptional character moment. Shaun's social anxiety and politeness are so ingrained that he apologises to a zombie and invites it to the pub. The 'if you're feeling better later' — treating zombieism as a mild illness — and the entirely sincere pub invite perfectly distil his character. Earns high craft scores for character integration and the earned quality of the humour — it's completely logical for this Shaun.

jokes.text: 'Pete'd be so pissed off if he knew I was driving his car.' / 'I don't think so.'
jokes.setup: Ed is gleefully driving Pete's car.
jokes.punchline: Ed revels in Pete's imagined anger; Shaun's quiet 'I don't think so' — knowing Pete is now a zombie and beyond caring — is a perfect understated dark joke.
jokes.explanation: Sharp dark comedy — Shaun's 'I don't think so' is the perfect understated delivery of 'because he's a zombie now.' The contrast between Ed's delight and Shaun's quiet correction is excellent.

jokes.text: Radio: 'The Church of England has joined other extremist religious groups in proclaiming this a sign of a coming apocalypse.'
jokes.setup: News report on zombie crisis mentions religious responses.
jokes.punchline: The Church of England is casually categorised as an 'extremist religious group' — a sly satirical jab at British institutional religion.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical aside — lumping the Church of England in with 'extremist religious groups' is a good British comedy joke about institutional religion. Low character integration because it's a writer's joke delivered by background radio.

jokes.text: They hit a zombie (or person) with the car. 'I think we hit something.' / 'Or someone.' / 'Ow!'
jokes.setup: Ed is driving erratically; they feel an impact.
jokes.punchline: 'Or someone' is the dark correction to Ed's optimistic 'something' — followed by an audible 'Ow!' from the victim, confirming the worst. The sequence of impact → polite reframing → evidence of human victim is perfectly timed.
jokes.explanation: Three-beat dark comedy: 'something' (euphemism) → 'or someone' (realism) → 'Ow!' (confirmation). Clean structure.

jokes.text: 'He's gonna be dead either way.' / 'That's not the point.'
jokes.setup: They've hit a person/zombie with the car and are deciding whether to stop. Ed argues they shouldn't bother.
jokes.punchline: 'He's gonna be dead either way' — Ed's cold logic is horrifyingly correct but delivered without any moral weight, then rebuked by Shaun's flustered 'That's not the point.'
jokes.explanation: Ed's nihilism is both funny and logically sound in-universe, which makes it unsettling and funny simultaneously. Shaun's moral objection 'that's not the point' is a straight-man moment that works because he's right, but Ed is also right.

jokes.text: They stop to check on the person they've hit; Shaun checks, says 'Oh, thank God for that' — apparently a zombie, so running them over was acceptable.
jokes.setup: Shaun gets out to check if they hit a living person.
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, thank God for that' — relief that the victim is a zombie, not a human. The moral calculus of zombie-world rendered in pure British relief.
jokes.explanation: Dark relief comedy — the inversion of normal moral concern (relief at running over a zombie) delivered with pious sincerity ('Oh, thank God'). Economical and effective.

jokes.text: 'Ah, hello.' / 'Who's a pretty boy then?' — Ed addressing a parrot at Barbara's house.
jokes.setup: They've arrived at Barbara's house, in survival mode.
jokes.punchline: Ed immediately stops to talk to a parrot, completely distracted from the mission.
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat — Ed distracted by a parrot mid-crisis is entirely consistent. Not a sharp joke but a good texture moment.

jokes.text: 'You didn't say Barbara had a Jag. I've always wanted to drive a Jag.' / 'It's Philip's. He won't let anybody near it. I put a Mars Bar in it once and he chased me with a bit of wood.'
jokes.setup: Ed spots Philip's prized Jaguar.
jokes.punchline: Shaun's backstory reveals Philip chased him with a piece of wood over a Mars Bar in his Jaguar — a perfectly specific piece of domestic absurdity that establishes Philip's character and the stepdad relationship.
jokes.explanation: The Mars Bar/wood anecdote is a great character-revealing detail — both funny in itself and doing real narrative work establishing Philip's character and Shaun's childhood grievances. 'A bit of wood' is a brilliantly specific weapon choice.

jokes.text: Ed volunteers to 'just look after the car' while Shaun goes in to deal with zombie Philip. 'If there's any problems, I'll honk three times.'
jokes.setup: Shaun and Ed arrive at Barbara's; there's dangerous zombie Philip inside.
jokes.punchline: Ed immediately finds a reason to stay outside with the car — 'just look after the car' — framing cowardice as responsible guard duty. 'I'll honk three times' establishes a signals protocol for staying out of danger.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ed cowardice dressed as practicality. The 'honk three times' protocol makes it formally ridiculous.

jokes.text: 'Don't forget to kill Philip!' — Ed shouting helpfully as Shaun approaches the house.
jokes.setup: Shaun is heading in to deal with zombie Philip.
jokes.punchline: Ed shouts this reminder cheerfully and loudly, as if Shaun might forget to murder his stepfather.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic beat — Ed shouting 'don't forget to kill Philip!' as cheerfully as a reminder to pick up milk. The casual framing of stepdad murder as a checklist item is very funny. High quotability.

jokes.text: 'You've got red on you.' — Barbara saying this to Shaun when he arrives, blood-spattered.
jokes.setup: Shaun arrives at his mum's house covered in zombie blood/gore.
jokes.punchline: Barbara greets him with the film's running gag — 'you've got red on you' — now delivered by a new character (Mum), proving the phrase is now the family's universal social-nicety register.
jokes.explanation: The running gag's third occurrence hits the hardest because it comes from Barbara, a new voice, proving the phrase is a cultural/family tic, not just Shaun and Ed's. The character integration score is 9.5 because only this specific family in this specific film would have this specific reflex. The escalating horror-to-normalcy contrast is at peak absurdity here.

jokes.text: Shaun enters with a cricket bat, trying to explain it's for killing zombie Philip. Philip: 'What have you got there? Flowers, I hope.' Shaun: 'No, it's... cricket bat.' 'Is that for the jumble, Shaun?'
jokes.setup: Shaun is trying to mercy-kill zombie Philip and has a cricket bat. Philip, in some intermediate zombie/lucid state, confronts him.
jokes.punchline: Philip assumes the cricket bat is for a jumble sale — an absurdly domestic interpretation of an apocalyptic weapon.
jokes.explanation: Philip's total obliviousness to the weapon's purpose (and to his own zombification) is a great character joke. 'Is that for the jumble, Shaun?' is the perfect suburban misreading of apocalyptic intent.

jokes.text: 'I took them all to the tip, Barbara.' — Philip correcting Barbara about Shaun's toys being upstairs, amid zombie crisis.
jokes.setup: Barbara mentions Shaun's toys are upstairs. Shaun is there to kill Philip.
jokes.punchline: Philip interjects to settle an ongoing domestic dispute about Shaun's toys — mid zombie apocalypse, mid attempted mercy killing — revealing the depth of mundane family tensions.
jokes.explanation: Good texture joke — Philip's mundane corrections to domestic disputes amid existential crisis is funny and character-revealing.

jokes.text: 'We had our jabs when we went to the Isle of Wight.' — Philip's rebuttal to zombie bite concerns.
jokes.setup: Shaun is trying to establish the danger of Philip's bite wound. Philip is dismissive.
jokes.punchline: Philip responds to zombie infection concern with 'we had our jabs when we went to the Isle of Wight' — treating zombie bite as a tropical disease preventable by routine holiday vaccinations.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best Philip jokes and a contender for the reel's funniest line.
