The specificity of 'Isle of Wight' (a quintessentially modest British holiday destination) combined with the confidence that standard travel jabs cover zombie infection is extraordinary. The character integration is 9 — only a certain generation of British stepfather would reason this way. 'It's overblown nonsense / a lot of drug nuts running wild' compounds it perfectly.

jokes.text: 'It's overblown nonsense. A lot of drug nuts running wild.'
jokes.setup: Philip dismisses the zombie apocalypse entirely.
jokes.punchline: His explanation for the zombie crisis is 'drug nuts running wild' — the most suburban, Daily Mail-reader explanation for the undead.
jokes.explanation: 'Drug nuts running wild' is superb character writing — it's the exact phrase a certain type of conservative older British man would use for any alarming social event. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'I haven't had sugar in my tea since 1982.'
jokes.setup: Barbara offers two sugars for Shaun's tea.
jokes.punchline: Shaun provides an absurdly precise date for when he gave up sugar — '1982' — suggesting he has never been asked this before or that his mum never remembers.
jokes.explanation: A quiet laugh — the specific year is funnier than 'a long time ago.' Works as a character beat revealing the domesticity trap Shaun can't escape even mid-apocalypse.

jokes.text: 'He chased me with a bit of wood!' / 'You did call him a you-know-what.' / 'Did he tell you that? Motherfucker.' / 'Shaun!' / 'Sorry, Mother... Mum!'
jokes.setup: Shaun tries to get Barbara to leave Philip by recounting Philip's cruelties. Barbara defends Philip by noting Shaun provoked him.
jokes.punchline: Shaun's outrage at Philip's betrayal causes him to say 'Motherfucker' directly to his mother — then immediately corrects to 'Mother... Mum!' in a spectacular self-correction.
jokes.explanation: The 'Mother... Mum!' self-correction is a perfectly crafted verbal slip joke. Shaun's horror at almost calling his mum a motherfucker is enhanced by the callback to Philip's wood-chasing. The mid-word redirect is impeccably timed and highly quotable. The craft is in the near-miss and the correction, not just the profanity.

jokes.text: 'Motherfucker.' / 'Shaun!' / 'Sorry, Mother... Mum!'
jokes.setup: Shaun is outraged that Philip told Barbara about being called a rude name. He erupts with 'Motherfucker.'
jokes.punchline: He immediately hears the word 'Mother' in 'Motherfucker' and self-corrects to 'Mum!' — a split-second verbal collision that reveals his panic.
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest wordplay gags in the film. The setup (Shaun swearing at Philip in outrage) leads to the punchline (he hears 'Mother' in his swear word mid-utterance and pivots to 'Mum!'). The structure is impeccable — it requires Shaun's specific relationship with Barbara to work, and the split-second correction is funnier than any deliberate joke. Truly excellent wordplay with perfect character integration. Comparable to a solid 8 anchor-level joke.

jokes.text: 'Did you know that on several occasions... he touched me?' (beat) 'That wasn't true. Made it up, shouldn't have, sorry.'
jokes.setup: Shaun is trying to convince Barbara to leave Philip, running out of legitimate grievances.
jokes.punchline: Shaun fabricates a serious accusation, there's a horrified beat, then he immediately recants: 'That wasn't true. Made it up, shouldn't have, sorry.' The speed of the confession makes it deeply funny.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely exceptional joke. Shaun's desperate fabrication of an abuse allegation followed by its instant deflation — 'that wasn't true. Made it up, shouldn't have, sorry' — is bold, dark, and perfectly executed. The beat between the accusation and the retraction is the entire joke. The speed of the confession is what makes it land as comedy rather than darkness. Character integration is 9 because only Shaun's specific combination of desperation, poor impulse control, and essential decency produces this exact sequence.

jokes.text: Philip, zombie-bitten and visibly declining, delivers a genuine 'there comes a time when you just gotta be a man' speech to Shaun — played completely straight.
jokes.setup: Shaun has failed to convince Barbara to leave. Philip, the man Shaun wanted to kill, intervenes with earnest life advice.
jokes.punchline: The irony that Philip — now partially zombified, the man Shaun planned to mercy-kill — is the one delivering the 'be a man' speech is darkly absurd. It's played completely straight, which makes it funnier and genuinely moving.
jokes.explanation: This is where the film's dark comedy and genuine emotion intersect most powerfully in this reel. The joke is structural — the dying/undead stepfather delivering the life lesson — but it's played with enough sincerity to also land emotionally. Lower impact score than craft because it's more of a tone beat than a laugh-out-loud moment, but its craft is exceptional.

jokes.text: 'Where's the car?' / 'Hmm... I pranged it.' / 'You were parked.'
jokes.setup: They emerge from the house to find Ed has had an accident with Pete's car.
jokes.punchline: Ed has managed to damage the car while simply parked — a feat of incompetence so pure it barely needs embellishment. 'You were parked' is the perfect straight-man response.
jokes.explanation: 'You were parked' is an exceptional comeback — the economy is perfect, the disbelief is implicit, and it makes the audience do the logical work (how do you crash a parked car?). The punchline earns its high score through supreme economy and structure.

jokes.text: 'Hmm... I pranged it.' / 'You were parked.' / 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Shaun emerges from his mum's house to find Ed has damaged Pete's car — while stationary.
jokes.punchline: 'You were parked.' Ed's admission that he managed to damage a parked car is delivered with almost impressed resignation by Shaun.
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat joke. The structure is clean: damage revealed → 'you were parked' as devastating understatement → Ed's flat 'yeah.' Three beats, no wasted words. 'You were parked' is a great line — it doesn't express anger, just quiet disbelief.

jokes.text: 'I guess we'll have to take the Jag.' — the logical consequence of the car being pranged.
jokes.setup: Pete's car is unusable. Philip (zombie) is coming with them. Philip's prized Jaguar — which 'he won't let anybody near' — is the only option.
jokes.punchline: Ed notes with barely concealed glee that they now have to take the Jag — the car Philip was so protective of that he chased Shaun with wood. Philip's imminent zombiehood negating all his car rules.
jokes.explanation: Good callback joke — Philip's car rules, so fiercely enforced, now completely irrelevant. The irony does most of the work.

jokes.text: 'Can you please turn that noise down?' — Philip, zombie-bitten and declining in the back seat of his own Jaguar, objecting to the music.
jokes.setup: They're driving through zombie apocalypse in Philip's Jaguar with Ed at the wheel.
jokes.punchline: Philip's dying concern is the music volume — the British instinct toward propriety and noise complaint survives even partial zombification.
jokes.explanation: Philip's character fully expressed in one complaint — the music noise bothers him more than being a zombie. The British propriety gag is well-executed and character-perfect.

jokes.text: 'Are you all right, dear? Would you like another tissue?' — Barbara fussing over zombie Philip like he has a cold.
jokes.setup: Philip is in the back of the Jaguar, turning into a zombie.
jokes.punchline: Barbara offers him a tissue — her maternal care instinct applied to a zombie husband, as if zombification is a sniffle.
jokes.explanation: Barbara's character joke — maternal fussing applied to zombie husband. The tissue offer is a perfect detail. Pairs beautifully with Philip's noise complaint as a double act of British propriety-in-crisis.

jokes.text: 'You do realise this is a 20 mile an hour zone?' — Philip, as zombie, correcting Ed's driving.
jokes.setup: They're racing through zombie-infested streets in the Jaguar.
jokes.punchline: Philip — turning into a zombie — interrupts the escape to enforce the speed limit. His most pressing concern during the zombie apocalypse is road safety compliance.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes and a genuine contender for the film's funniest character moment. The specificity — 20 mile an hour zone, not just 'slow down' — combined with the absolute priorities inversion (speed limit > zombie apocalypse) is pitch-perfect character comedy. Only this specific type of British man would die worrying about road safety compliance. The character integration is 9.5. This is the kind of joke that makes the film great.

jokes.text: 'Have you still got the child locks on?' / 'Safety first, Shaun.'
jokes.setup: Shaun is trying to get out of the Jaguar but can't open the door.
jokes.punchline: Barbara has the child locks on — in the middle of a zombie escape — prioritising road safety over emergency exit. 'Safety first, Shaun' delivered with complete maternal sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Perfect companion joke to the 20mph zone — the whole Jaguar scene is a sustained comedic masterpiece of British propriety overriding apocalypse. 'Safety first, Shaun' is both funny and completely in character for Barbara. High quotability.

jokes.text: 'Hey, man, watch the leather.' — Philip's last coherent concern as he zombifies.
jokes.setup: Shaun is scrambling around the Jaguar trying to exit while Philip turns into a zombie.
jokes.punchline: Philip's final lucid words are a complaint about Shaun scuffing the leather seats — his car's upholstery mattering more than the undead apocalypse or his own mortality.
jokes.explanation: Among the film's finest jokes and the crowning moment of this reel. 'Watch the leather' as a dying man's final coherent words — delivered presumably as zombie transformation takes hold — is a perfect crystallisation of everything the film does. It's a callback to Philip's car obsession, a character joke of the highest order, dark comedy operating at peak, and an absurdist triumph. The character integration is 10/10 — no other character in any other film could say this line. The economy (three words) earns maximum score. This is the reel's best joke.

jokes.text: 'Keep moving. If there's any problems... I'll do the honks.' — Ed reprising his car-guard protocol, now with the Jaguar.
jokes.setup: Ed is staying behind (again) with the car. Earlier he established 'I'll honk three times' as the signal.
jokes.punchline: Ed has downgraded from 'I'll honk three times' to 'I'll do the honks' — a vague, non-committal version of his own protocol. Also reprises the cowardice-as-practicality joke.
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the downgrade from 'three honks' to 'do the honks' is a subtle character joke about Ed's commitment levels. Closes the reel with a small running gag payoff.

jokes.text: "Oh, you made a plan?" — Liz's withering, incredulous response to Shaun announcing he has a plan
jokes.setup: Shaun bursts in heroically declaring he has come to save everyone and has a plan
jokes.punchline: Liz's flat, sarcastic echo of 'you made a plan' perfectly skewers his prior unreliability and punctures his hero entrance
jokes.explanation: Works on two levels: it's a believable human reaction AND it encapsulates their whole relationship dynamic in three words. The economy is exceptional — four words do the work of an entire backstory.

jokes.text: "And that will exacerbate things for all of us." — Shaun's bizarrely formal word choice while describing being torn apart by zombies
jokes.setup: Shaun is urgently warning everyone that zombies will tear them to pieces
jokes.punchline: He uses the clinical, almost academic word 'exacerbate' in the middle of a visceral zombie survival speech, exposing his slightly pretentious everyman quality
jokes.explanation: Classic Edgar Wright tonal whiplash — the word is hilariously out of register with the mortal peril being described. It also characterises Shaun as someone who half-read a thesaurus. Easy to miss on first watch, plays better on rewatch.

jokes.text: Dianne immediately sides with Shaun; then immediately in the same breath says she's not going outside.
jokes.setup: Shaun gives his rousing survival speech and asks for support.
jokes.punchline: Dianne declares 'We're with you, Shaun!' then in the very next line refuses to go outside, completely contradicting herself.
jokes.explanation: Quick-fire self-contradiction gag that lands on character (the hangers-on who want to signal support without actually committing). The beat-for-beat turnaround in the same breath is what makes it work.

jokes.text: "All right, Flash, what's your plan?" — David's sarcastic nickname for Shaun
jokes.setup: Shaun has just delivered a rousing 'we're all in this together' speech
jokes.punchline: David immediately deflates it with a withering 'Flash Gordon' diminutive, signalling his default contrarianism
jokes.explanation: Economical character work. 'Flash' is both mockery of Shaun's delusions of grandeur and a perfect capture of David's snide personality. Works better in context than in isolation.

jokes.text: "Yes! Great. Where?" / "Oh, no. Well, I've passed my test." / "David?" / "I don't see the point of owning a car in London."
jokes.setup: Shaun asks if anyone has transport, someone says yes, raising hopes
jokes.punchline: The answer deflates immediately — the person who said yes only means they have a licence, not a car; David smugly invokes the 'no car in London' cliché as his excuse, turning a practical crisis into an absurd non-answer
jokes.explanation: Triple-beat escalating disappointment executed with great rhythm: hope (Yes!) → query (Great, where?) → deflation (I've passed my test) → further deflation (David's smug London non-answer). Each beat lands. The structure alone elevates this above a simple one-liner.

jokes.text: "So, what's the plan, then?" after Shaun has just finished explaining the plan
jokes.setup: Shaun has just laid out a clear, succinct plan: get blunt objects, bash heads, stay together, follow him
jokes.punchline: Ed immediately asks 'So, what's the plan, then?' as if he wasn't listening at all — a perfect expression of Ed's cheerful uselessness
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes. Entirely dependent on character — no other person in the group could deliver this. The timing (immediate, zero pause) is perfect. It compresses Ed's entire personality into four words. The absence of self-awareness is funnier than any deliberate joke could be. Justifiably scores 8+: it has the economy and character integration of the anchor examples.

jokes.text: "What's up, niggaz?" — Ed's greeting to the group from the car
jokes.setup: The group has been anxiously waiting for transport during a zombie crisis
jokes.punchline: Ed arrives and greets them with the most casually inappropriate slang possible, treating the apocalypse like a school pickup
jokes.explanation: Classic Ed obliviousness. The tonal mismatch (apocalyptic dread vs. casual bro greeting) is the joke. Character-specific, economical, though the word choice is a touch dated.

jokes.text: "Is your dad all right?" / "He's not my dad." — the running gag about Philip
jokes.setup: Philip is bleeding in the back seat; Liz, trying to be helpful, calls him Shaun's dad
jokes.punchline: Shaun's reflexive, prickly correction that Philip is his stepfather, not his dad — even in a crisis
jokes.explanation: The joke accumulates value as a running gag. By this point in the film, the audience anticipates the correction, making it a Pavlovian payoff. Gets funnier each repetition because the circumstances become more inappropriate.

jokes.text: "Thought you wanted to get there fast?" — Ed's response to being told to be careful
jokes.setup: Shaun tells Ed to get to the Winchester fast, then immediately tells him to be careful as he drives dangerously
jokes.punchline: Ed cheekily points out the contradiction in real time
jokes.explanation: Quick, clean comedic logic. Ed's literal-mindedness is consistent with his character. Not a standout but functional, well-timed.

jokes.text: "Big Al also says dogs can't look up." / "They can't." / "Can't they?" / "Of course they can!" / "Are you sure?"
jokes.setup: Shaun invokes 'Big Al' as an authority on the pub's rifle being active ('Big Al says so')
jokes.punchline: Liz undermines the Big Al authority chain by citing his ludicrous claim that dogs can't look up — but then Ed and Shaun's genuine uncertainty about whether dogs CAN look up completely derails the conversation during a life-or-death escape
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's true standouts and among the most quoted moments in the film. The genius is the pivot: Liz deploys the dog fact to deflate Big Al's credibility, but Shaun and Ed's genuine, dawning uncertainty ('Are you sure?') turns it into something far funnier — an absurdist tangent in the middle of an apocalypse that perfectly captures their intellectual limitations. Earns 8+ for originality, perfect economy, and the multi-layer structure where the second beat (genuine doubt) is funnier than the first.

jokes.text: "I turned it off, all right?" — Shaun's cryptic response to Liz saying his name
jokes.setup: Liz says 'Shaun' in an apparent attempt to get his attention mid-argument; Philip is bleeding in the back; everyone expects another argument beat
jokes.punchline: Shaun pre-emptively snaps 'I turned it off, all right?' — clearly guilty about something (his phone), and completely wrong about what Liz was about to say; the non-sequitur is baffling and funny
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-constructed misdirection. Shaun's defensive guilt reads clearly; the fact that Liz wasn't even asking about his phone makes his confession funnier. Slight rewatch value as you notice his preemptive guilt.

jokes.text: Philip's deathbed speech — 'You were 12 when I met you' — delivered while zombified and bleeding in a moving car
jokes.setup: Philip has been bitten and is slowly turning; the car is in chaos; everyone is trying to survive
jokes.punchline: Philip chooses this moment for a long-overdue heart-to-heart with Shaun, delivering a tender, sincere fatherly speech while visibly dying from a zombie bite — the earnestness of the speech against the grotesque context is the joke
jokes.explanation: Edgar Wright weaponises sincerity. The scene is genuinely moving AND funny simultaneously, which is very hard to pull off. The horror-comedy tension peaks here: Philip's earnest love for Shaun is completely real, and that's precisely what makes the context so darkly hilarious. Earns 8+ for the tonal ambition and the courage to make the audience feel something while laughing.

jokes.text: Ed's driving causes everyone to lurch; Liz screams at Ed to stop; Ed: 'Chill out. Everyone's all right.' / 'Stop telling me to chill out! And everybody is not all right.'
jokes.setup: Philip has just died/turned in the backseat; the car has lurched dangerously.
jokes.punchline: Ed's breezy 'Chill out, everyone's all right' — when Philip is a zombie in the back — is a monumental misjudgement that earns Liz's explosion.
jokes.explanation: Ed's obliviousness to the seriousness of events is a running character engine. 'Chill out, everyone's all right' while a zombie is literally in the car is a great character-driven irony beat.

jokes.text: "Mum, it's Philip, he's gone." / "Where's he gone?" / "Mum, he's dead." / "No, he isn't."
jokes.setup: Shaun tries to gently inform his mother that her husband has died/turned
jokes.punchline: Barbara's first response — 'Where's he gone?' — is both literal and painfully oblivious; her second — 'No, he isn't' — is the flat denial of someone who simply cannot process it. Neither is played for laughs by the character, which makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Barbara's denial is both a believable grief reaction and a perfect comedy beat. 'No, he isn't' in flat defiance of an obvious zombie-death is classically British in its refusal to acknowledge bad news. Dark, earned, character-specific.

jokes.text: Philip zombified in the car — physical struggle to escape the car with child locks engaged
jokes.setup: Philip has turned into a zombie in the backseat of the car
jokes.punchline: The group cannot escape because Ed engaged the child locks, turning a horrifying zombie attack into a farcical car-safety issue
jokes.explanation: The child-lock detail is a masterclass in Edgar Wright's specificity of comedy — it's not just 'zombie in car,' it's 'zombie in car and you can't get out because of child locks.' The mundane domestic safety feature defeating the group is both hilarious and structurally brilliant. Earns 8+ for the specificity of the comedic idea and its escalating panic.

jokes.text: "We can't leave your dad." / "He's not my dad!" — repeated even now
jokes.setup: The group has just barely escaped the zombie version of Philip
jokes.punchline: Even after the traumatic zombie attack, David refers to Philip as Shaun's dad, triggering the reflexive correction in the most inappropriate possible moment
jokes.explanation: The running gag accumulates power here because the context is genuinely horrifying. Shaun still cannot stop himself from making the correction, which is perfect character comedy. The gag earns its place by paying off differently each time.

jokes.text: "That's not your husband in there. OK? It looks like him but there is nothing of the man you loved in that car." — Shaun's sincere comfort, undercut by the mundane phrase 'in that car'
jokes.setup: Shaun is trying to console his grieving mother that zombie-Philip is not really Philip
jokes.punchline: The speech is almost eloquent until 'in that car' — a perfectly prosaic, undignified final phrase that gently punctures the moment
jokes.explanation: Wright and Pegg's gift for bathos. Shaun almost achieves real eloquence, then the sentence lands in the most practical and therefore funny place. The joke is subtle — many audiences laugh while also feeling moved.

jokes.text: "You're not suggesting we walk?" — after losing the car
jokes.setup: The group has just abandoned the car with a zombie Philip in it and must continue to the Winchester
jokes.punchline: David's indignation at the prospect of walking — during a zombie apocalypse — perfectly captures his oblivious privilege
jokes.explanation: David's complaint is perfectly character-specific: the man who 'doesn't see the point of owning a car in London' now protests walking. His middle-class uselessness in a crisis is a consistent comic vein the film mines well.

jokes.text: "Yeah, we're having a whale of a time." — Liz's response when asked if everyone is OK
jokes.setup: Shaun asks 'Everybody OK?' after the traumatic car escape from zombie-Philip
jokes.punchline: Liz's perfectly dry sarcasm — 'we're having a whale of a time' — could not be more British or more perfectly calibrated
jokes.explanation: Economy is perfect. 'Whale of a time' is a specifically British idiom that lands with perfect deadpan timing. Liz has quietly been the reel's best straight-man/reactor.

jokes.text: "Maybe we should all hold hands, make a crocodile?" — Dianne's suggestion for the group walk
jokes.setup: The group is shuffling nervously through zombie-infested streets
jokes.punchline: Dianne — who is played as enthusiastically dim — suggests the group form a school-outing crocodile line, treating the apocalypse with the energy of a primary school teacher
jokes.explanation: Perfectly character-specific absurdism from Dianne. 'Make a crocodile' is such a specific, British primary-school phrase that it becomes funny precisely through that specificity.

jokes.text: Yvonne's parallel group mirror scene — Yvonne has an identical group including a boyfriend, friends, her mum and a cousin, all with the same energy
jokes.setup: Shaun and his ragtag group stumble into Yvonne's group mid-escape
jokes.punchline: Yvonne's group is a conspicuously well-organised parallel to Shaun's group — same composition (boyfriend, friends, mum, cousin), heading somewhere else, moving with actual competence — the joke is the contrast
jokes.explanation: A visual structural joke — Yvonne is Shaun's competent mirror image. Her group works, his doesn't. The parallel construction is funny on its own but also quietly satirises how differently people perform in a crisis.

jokes.text: "Right, well. Good luck!" — Yvonne's breezy farewell as she heads off with her competent group
jokes.setup: Shaun tells Yvonne they're going to the Winchester pub; she clearly thinks it's a terrible idea
jokes.punchline: Her 'Good luck!' is so breezy and so final — she doesn't even try to change his mind. The understatement is devastating.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — two words that say everything. Yvonne is not rude, not unkind, she just knows Shaun well enough that 'Good luck!' with that tone is a complete judgement.

jokes.text: The awkward wave sequence — 'Hi / Hello / Hi / Hello / All right' between the two groups
jokes.setup: The two groups have finished their conversation and need to part ways
jokes.punchline: Instead of a clean exit, the two groups exchange a lengthy, multiply-repeated round of polite hellos/goodbyes, with no one willing to break away first — classic British social awkwardness in a zombie apocalypse
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most purely British comic moments. The 'Hi / Hello / Hi / Hello / All right' rhythm is perfectly observed — everyone has experienced this exact social loop. That it happens while fleeing zombies is the entire joke. Earns its score for the universality of the observation deployed in an absurd context.

jokes.text: "Just over there, over the 20 garden fences?" — David's incredulous reaction to Shaun's shortcut
jokes.setup: Shaun points to the Winchester 'just over there'
jokes.punchline: David's specific count of 'twenty garden fences' — an instantly visual exaggeration that is also probably accurate — perfectly skewers Shaun's optimistic geography
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '20 fences' rather than 'loads of fences' makes this joke. It instantly creates a visual of exactly how ridiculous Shaun's shortcut is. David's pedantry, usually annoying, here functions as perfect comic observation.

jokes.text: "What's the matter, David? Never taken a short cut before?"
jokes.setup: David has just pointed out the absurdity of climbing over 20 garden fences
jokes.punchline: Shaun's breezy dismissal — delivered with genuine bafflement at David's hesitation — is funny because Shaun is apparently the only person who thinks this is normal
jokes.explanation: Good beat in the rhythm of the scene but not exceptional on its own. Shaun's oblivious confidence is funny; the line itself is merely functional.

jokes.text: "One, two, three, four, five. Yes." / "There's six of us." — Shaun miscounts the group
jokes.setup: Shaun does a headcount of the group before proceeding
jokes.punchline: He confidently announces there are five, immediately contradicted — he forgot to count himself (or someone else)
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom beat — the leader cannot even count his own group. Quick, clean, works in context. Nothing special but executed competently.

jokes.text: Barbara wanders off and falls while Shaun is mid-headcount
jokes.setup: Shaun has just finished his headcount and told everyone to stay where they are
jokes.punchline: Barbara immediately wanders off and apparently falls, negating his instruction the second it's given
jokes.explanation: Physical gag relying on the 'everyone ignore Shaun's instructions immediately' pattern. Functional escalation of his inability to lead. Barbara's oblivious warmth makes it gentler than it would otherwise be.

jokes.text: "I don't think Jill and Derek do live here." — Barbara's observation after falling in a stranger's garden
jokes.setup: Barbara had suggested 'Jill and Derek live round here' as they cut through gardens; she has now fallen
jokes.punchline: After the fall — having caused a minor disaster — Barbara's conclusion is the supremely understated 'I don't think Jill and Derek do live here', delivered as if this was simply a navigation error
jokes.explanation: Perfect British understatement. Barbara's quiet conclusion — delivered as a mild geographical update rather than a reaction to chaos — is exactly how her character processes events. The 'do live here' phrasing is especially English and funny. Earns 8+ for character integration, economy, and the perfect callback structure all in one line.

jokes.text: After being rescued from a zombie in a garden: 'I don't think Jill and Derek do live here.'
jokes.setup: Barbara had mused that Jill and Derek might live in one of these gardens (joke 22); she wandered off and apparently encountered a zombie or hazard.
jokes.punchline: Her conclusion, calmly delivered after what was clearly a frightening encounter, is simply that she was wrong about the address.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the finest jokes in the film and among the best callback structures in British comedy. The setup (57:40) is innocuous and easily forgotten; Barbara's wandering creates a visual slapstick interlude; and then she pays it all off with supreme understatement about the wrong address. The word economy is extraordinary — nine words resolve what could have been a screaming scene. The character specificity is perfect: only Barbara would process a zombie encounter as a navigation correction. Easily one of the standout moments of this reel and the entire film.

jokes.text: Garden zombie fight — Shaun fights a zombie while group watches; 'Feel free to step in any time.' / 'You did all right.' / 'I didn't want to cramp your style.'
jokes.setup: Shaun has just had to physically fight off a zombie while the group stood and watched
jokes.punchline: Ed's excuse for not helping — 'I didn't want to cramp your style' — is both absurd and perfectly Ed: he watched his friend battle a zombie and interpreted it as a solo performance
jokes.explanation: 'I didn't want to cramp your style' is one of the film's most quotable lines. The reframing of zombie-combat as a stylistic performance that Ed was politely leaving Shaun to is so specifically absurd and so specifically Ed that it earns its high score. Justifies 8+ for the same reasons as the anchor examples: unexpected angle, perfect economy, could only be this character.

jokes.text: "Is it clear?" / "No." / "How many?" / "Lots."
jokes.setup: Shaun scouts ahead to check if the Winchester's approach is clear
jokes.punchline: His return report to himself (or to the group) is simply 'No' and 'Lots' — the most deflationary possible update after all the effort to get there
jokes.explanation: Economy is the entire joke. 'Lots' as the final word after everything the group has endured to get there is perfectly timed and perfectly flat. The rhythm of question/answer works like a double act.

jokes.text: "Because... Because, because of... Captain Wow."
jokes.setup: David is asked why he left his safe flat to come with Shaun; he was the most resistant member of the group
jokes.punchline: His answer, after multiple false starts, is 'Captain Wow' — presumably a sarcastic nickname for Shaun — but the hesitation and deflation of the build-up landing on this absurd label is funnier than any straight answer would have been
jokes.explanation: 'Captain Wow' lands because the build-up promises a genuine emotional admission and delivers a petty nickname instead. The cadence — 'because... because, because of...' — sells the punchline. Surprisingly quotable.

jokes.text: "Right, let's all shake out. Get nice and limber." — Shaun's pre-zombie-impersonation warm-up
jokes.setup: The group needs to pass through a zombie horde by impersonating zombies
jokes.punchline: Shaun treats the zombie impersonation like a sports team warm-up, calling for everyone to 'get nice and limber' — the PE-teacher energy is entirely wrong for the situation
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the zombie-walk sequence. Shaun's misapplication of team-sports energy to a zombie scenario is consistent with his character. Functional comedy that serves the scene well.

jokes.text: "Almost like sleepwalking. Look at the face, it's vacant with a hint of sadness. Like a drunk who's lost a bet."
jokes.setup: Shaun is coaching the group on how to impersonate zombies by studying one
jokes.punchline: His description of zombie movement — culminating in 'like a drunk who's lost a bet' — is both accurate and hilariously specific
jokes.explanation: 'Like a drunk who's lost a bet' is one of the film's great lines — an absurdly specific and yet entirely accurate description of zombie movement that could only come from British pub culture. The build ('vacant... hint of sadness... like a drunk') is a perfect three-part structure leading to a killer specific image. Fully earns 8+ for originality, economy, and quotability.

jokes.text: "Nice. Good vocal work." — Shaun critiquing Liz's zombie impression like a drama teacher
jokes.setup: Shaun is directing the group's zombie impressions
jokes.punchline: He praises Liz's performance with the vocabulary of a drama school tutor — 'Good vocal work' — during an apocalypse
jokes.explanation: Part of the sustained comedy of the zombie-direction scene. Shaun as accidental drama teacher is funny; this specific line is good but slightly overshadowed by the stronger lines in the same sequence.

jokes.text: "Sorry, dear, I was miles away." — Barbara, apparently having zoned out during zombie coaching
jokes.setup: Shaun is urgently coaching everyone to impersonate zombies for survival; calls on Barbara
jokes.punchline: Barbara apologises as if she'd drifted off in a tea room rather than during a survival exercise, with 'I was miles away' as the most gently oblivious excuse possible
jokes.explanation: Barbara's 'I was miles away' is perfect character comedy — it's exactly what this woman would say in this moment, and that specificity is what makes it work. Her cheerful obliviousness to danger is consistently funny.

jokes.text: "I'll do it on the night." — Ed refusing to rehearse his zombie impression
jokes.setup: Shaun asks Ed to demonstrate his zombie impression; everyone else has done theirs
jokes.punchline: Ed declines with the excuse of an actor saving their energy for the actual performance — except THIS IS the actual night, as Shaun immediately points out
jokes.explanation: 'I'll do it on the night' / 'This is the night!' — a perfect two-beat. Ed's theatrical prima-donna logic (saving it for the performance) in a situation where rehearsal is life-or-death survival is a brilliant character-comedy construction. Earns high score for the structure and character integration: only Ed would use this exact excuse.

jokes.text: "Who died and made you fucking king of the zombies?" — Ed's explosive protest to Shaun's zombie direction
jokes.setup: Shaun is acting as director/leader of the zombie-impersonation exercise; Ed is not cooperating
jokes.punchline: Ed adapts the classic 'who died and made you king?' idiom with 'king of the zombies' — a brilliant accidental pun given that they're literally surrounded by the undead; the anger is also disproportionately funny
jokes.explanation: The reel's single best joke. The idiom 'who died and made you king?' adapted to 'king of the zombies' is a perfect wordplay-pun that works on multiple levels: (1) it's literally asking about death in a film about the undead, (2) the idiom and the scenario collide perfectly, (3) Ed's genuine indignation makes it feel unscripted, (4) it's maximally quotable. This is the kind of joke that becomes part of a film's cultural identity. Five words, perfectly placed. Scores among the best wordplay in British film comedy — genuinely comparable to the craft anchor examples.

jokes.text: "Yeah, that's pretty good." — Shaun's reluctant admission after Ed's angry outburst counts as a zombie impression
jokes.setup: Ed has just screamed 'Who died and made you fucking king of the zombies?' at Shaun in genuine fury
jokes.punchline: Shaun's calm, grudging '...yeah, that's pretty good' — evaluating the screamed outburst as a valid zombie impression — is the perfect button on the previous joke
jokes.explanation: Four words that extend and double the previous joke. Shaun appraising genuine anger as 'pretty good' (not even 'great') shows his absolute refusal to break the director frame. The understatement ('pretty good', not 'perfect') is funnier than a compliment would be. The two jokes (40 and 41) are functionally a single brilliant two-beat sequence.

jokes.text: "John? John, Bernie, are you there? It's Shaun and Ed. We come in all the time." — Shaun calling through zombie-infested pub door
jokes.setup: The group has made it to the Winchester but zombies are everywhere and the pub appears closed
jokes.punchline: Shaun shouts through the door using his regular-customer credentials — 'we come in all the time' — as if the barmen might just be doing a normal stock-take and need convincing
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the category error — using social capital ('we're regulars') as a survival tool. It's beautifully specific to Shaun's pub attachment.

jokes.text: "We do the quiz." — added credential while banging on the zombie-besieged pub door
jokes.setup: Shaun is trying to establish their regular-customer credentials to get into the Winchester
jokes.punchline: Ed adds 'We do the quiz' as an additional credential — as if quiz night attendance is the decisive factor
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'we come in all the time' to 'we do the quiz' is perfect British pub comedy. Quiz-night regulars are a specific tribe, and Ed invoking it with total sincerity is exactly right. Very economical, very character-specific.

jokes.text: "Fuck fucking off! I've spent an entire life sticking up for you and all you ever do is fuck things up and make me look stupid."
jokes.setup: Ed has broken the zombie-walk disguise by taking a phone call at the worst possible moment
jokes.punchline: Shaun's explosive, articulate, years-of-frustration dressing-down — 'Fuck fucking off!' as opener, then a full accounting of their friendship — erupts while surrounded by zombies, and is funny both for the content and the timing
jokes.explanation: 'Fuck fucking off' as a novel intensification of the standard expletive is funny on its own. The context — this is not the moment for home truths — makes it funnier. Shaun's pent-up articulate fury landing here is both earned drama and great comedy.

jokes.text: Shaun explodes at Ed: 'You stupid moron. Fuck off. You fuck off! Fuck fucking off!' — escalating profanity spiral.
jokes.setup: Ed has just blown their zombie camouflage cover by making a phone call; Shaun is furious.
jokes.punchline: The 'fuck off' exchange escalates from a standard insult into 'Fuck fucking off!' — grammatical nonsense that shows Shaun's anger has overwhelmed his syntax.
jokes.explanation: 'Fuck fucking off' is a lovely escalation joke — the syntax has broken down under emotional pressure. The subsequent speech ('I've spent my entire life sticking up for you') gives it emotional weight, making the explosion funnier because it's also real. Good comic-to-emotional bridge.

jokes.text: "You were saying about another way in?" — Shaun, completely calm, immediately after his explosive rant
jokes.setup: Shaun has just delivered a full emotional breakdown at Ed; the moment is charged
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots back to practical problem-solving as if nothing happened — 'You were saying about another way in?' — the contrast between emotional explosion and instant practicality is perfectly British
jokes.explanation: One of the best laugh-beats in the reel. The speed of the pivot from raw emotional outburst to calm logistics is a perfect example of British repression comedy. Earns 8+ for the structural perfection of the button — it simultaneously resolves the anger AND advances the plot, which is very hard to do with a single line.

jokes.text: "Come on, you pasty-faced fuckers, let's go! Follow me." / "Come and get it. It's a running buffet. All you can eat!"
jokes.setup: Ed is attempting to draw the zombie horde away from the Winchester so the group can get inside
jokes.punchline: Ed's zombie-taunting patter — 'running buffet, all you can eat!' — frames himself as the meal with the energy of a cheerful market stallholder, which is both heroic and completely Ed
jokes.explanation: 'Running buffet' and 'all you can eat' reframe Ed as willing human food with cheerful market-trader energy. It's heroic self-sacrifice described in the least heroic terms possible — classic Ed. The character specificity is perfect.

jokes.text: "I think they're for me." — Barbara about flowers left in the pub
jokes.setup: The group finally enters the Winchester; Barbara spots some flowers
jokes.punchline: Barbara assumes the flowers are for her — a completely unfounded, sweetly delusional conclusion that shows her total disconnection from the situation
jokes.explanation: Barbara's sweet narcissism — entirely benign, entirely believable — is funny because of how perfectly it ignores context. 'I think they're for me' in a zombie-besieged pub is a perfect character beat.

jokes.text: "I'm sure he'll knock." — David's flippant response to 'How will Shaun get back in?' after window is smashed
jokes.setup: The group debates whether to block the smashed window; someone asks how Shaun will get back in
jokes.punchline: David's 'I'm sure he'll knock' is delivered with utter confidence about something completely obvious — but the deadpan certainty of it, as if this resolves everything, is funny
jokes.explanation: Quick, competent beat. David's smug confidence is consistent but the joke itself is fairly predictable. Works in the rhythm of the scene.

jokes.text: "You did that, you twat." — Liz to David about the smashed window he's now worried about
jokes.setup: David is now complaining about the exposed broken window as a security risk
jokes.punchline: Liz reminds him he was the one who smashed it — a clean, deserved rebuke that lands because David is oblivious to his own role in problems he then complains about
jokes.explanation: 'You did that, you twat' is a beautifully efficient callback. The word 'twat' lands with specifically British sharpness. Liz as David's designated deflater is a consistent comic dynamic that the film has earned.

jokes.text: David's speech about taking control / responsibility — building to 'then perhaps... I should.'
jokes.setup: David is building up to a heroic declaration about leadership
jokes.punchline: The speech builds with genuine portent but lands on 'then perhaps... I should' — the most self-important, least warranted claim to authority possible from a man who just smashed a window and immediately regretted it
jokes.explanation: Classic pompous-character comedy. David's self-regard is perfectly out of proportion to his actual usefulness. The dramatic pause before 'I should' is very good structure.

jokes.text: "A man whose idea of a romantic nightspot is also an impenetrable fortress. This is a pub! We are in a pub!"
jokes.setup: David is critiquing Shaun's choice of the Winchester
jokes.punchline: The observation that a pub serving as both romantic venue AND survival fortress is absurd has actual comic truth to it — 'this is a pub!' as an indignant revelation is funny because it's both correct and completely misses the point
jokes.explanation: David is inadvertently making the film's thesis point — the Winchester IS Shaun's answer to everything — while thinking he's making a critique. The dramatic 'This is a pub!' lands well.

jokes.text: "I could get a round in." — Ed's response to David's 'What are we going to do?' speech
jokes.setup: David has delivered a passionate speech about their hopeless situation: no lights, no power, they're in a pub
jokes.punchline: Ed's response to existential crisis is to offer to get a round in — the most on-brand, perfectly timed deflation of David's speech possible
jokes.explanation: Five words that could only come from Ed. The entire film's thesis — the pub as refuge, Ed as the man who can always find the positive in alcohol — compressed into one perfectly timed line. David's speech sets up genuine dread; Ed punctures it with absolute cheerful practicality. This is what 8.5+ looks like: perfect character integration, maximal economy, the right line at exactly the right moment.

jokes.text: "Toasties! There's a Breville out back." / "Great. Saved by nibbles."
jokes.setup: David despairs about what they'll eat; Dianne offers a solution
jokes.punchline: Dianne's solution is a Breville sandwich toaster; David's withering 'Saved by nibbles' treats it as farcically inadequate
jokes.explanation: Good comic rhythm. 'Breville' as the pivot between despair and bathos is very British. David's 'Saved by nibbles' is snobbish and funny.

jokes.text: 'Ed, get me a double vodka.' / 'Right you are.'
jokes.setup: David's catastrophizing speech has been going on for some time and Liz finally cracks.
jokes.punchline: Liz's response to existential zombie crisis is a double vodka. Ed's 'right you are' — as if he's behind the bar on a normal night — is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Ed's 'right you are' as if everything is normal is a good beat. The joke is in the normalization — in a pub, the response to stress is a drink, and that logic holds even in a zombie apocalypse.

jokes.text: "Right, great, fuck it. We'll have a party and get completely smashed."
jokes.setup: Ed announces he's getting a double vodka; everyone agrees to have a drink
jokes.punchline: David's indignant 'Right, great, fuck it, we'll have a party' is the satirical response of a man who's lost control of a situation — his sarcasm doesn't stop anyone and makes him look even more helpless
jokes.explanation: David's futile indignation is consistent comedy. The joke is that his sarcasm changes nothing — everyone ignores him.

jokes.text: "Yeah, well, I promised, didn't I?" — Shaun's return to the Winchester
jokes.setup: Shaun has returned after what felt like an impossibly long absence; Liz had earlier questioned whether he'd come back
jokes.punchline: His explanation for returning is characteristically low-key — 'I promised, didn't I?' — with the casual implication that keeping promises in a zombie apocalypse is simply what you do
jokes.explanation: The understatement of this return — no heroics, just 'I promised' — is entirely consistent with Shaun's character and the film's comedic register. Sweet without being saccharine.

jokes.text: Shaun returns: 'Yeah, well, I promised, didn't I?' — casual, as if popping out for milk.
jokes.setup: Liz has just defended Shaun saying he wouldn't abandon them; David doubted it. Shaun reappears.
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah, well, I promised, didn't I?' — delivered with minimal fanfare, treating a death-defying return from a zombie horde as a simple matter of keeping one's word.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Shaun moment. The understatement of 'I promised, didn't I?' — treating life-threatening zombie evasion as a point of honour about keeping promises — is true to his character and genuinely touching and funny simultaneously. The 'didn't I?' adds a slight defiance that's very human.

jokes.text: "I just gave them the slip. Wasn't difficult. They're not all that." — Shaun dismissing the zombie horde
jokes.setup: Everyone wants to know how Shaun escaped from the massive zombie horde he led away
jokes.punchline: His breezy dismissal — 'They're not all that' — treats the zombie apocalypse with the contempt of someone who found the difficulty slightly beneath them
jokes.explanation: 'They're not all that' as zombie dismissal is perfectly pitched British understatement. Shaun's growing competence is played with just enough self-deprecation to stay funny.

jokes.text: "Well, how did you get in?" / "The back door." / "I tried to tell you before you smashed the window. But it wasn't me blowing our cover by arguing with my boyfriend."
jokes.setup: Everyone is amazed Shaun got in; they all struggled with the smashed window
jokes.punchline: Shaun reveals the back door was always there — he tried to tell them — and then can't resist the pointed callback to Liz calling Ed his 'boyfriend' (echoing their own argument)
jokes.explanation: Double callback: the back door vindicating Shaun, AND the 'boyfriend' echo. The layering rewards attentive viewers. Shaun's restraint in just barely making the point rather than rubbing it in is funny and consistent.

jokes.text: "Might be a bit warm, the cooler's off." — Shaun, handing Ed a beer immediately after
jokes.setup: After exposing Liz and David's role in the window disaster, Shaun hands Ed a beer
jokes.punchline: His only caveat about the warm beer is completely casual — the cooler's off is merely a mild inconvenience he mentions in passing — signals they are now simply pub regulars who happen to be in an apocalypse
jokes.explanation: Sweet, quick beat. The normalisation of pub behaviour within crisis is consistent with the film's thesis. Not a standout but pleasant.

jokes.text: "Would anyone like a peanut?" — Shaun's response to 'what's the plan'
jokes.setup: Ed asks Shaun what the plan is now they're in the Winchester
jokes.punchline: Shaun offers peanuts. That IS the plan. The apocalypse plan was always to get to the pub and have a pint and a snack.
jokes.explanation: The reel's highest-craft joke and arguably the film's thesis statement in four words. It simultaneously (1) answers Ed's question with brutal honesty, (2) validates David's earlier sarcasm about the plan being 'eating peanuts', (3) pays off the entire Winchester-as-sanctuary running joke from reel 1, and (4) is delivered with such perfect deadpan that the audience can choose to read it as defeat OR contentment. The economy is perfect 10 — no word can be removed. The structure is a full-film callback landing here. Among the best single lines in British comedy cinema.

jokes.text: "Why don't you do your Clyde?" — Ed suggesting his orang-utan impression from Every Which Way But Loose
jokes.setup: The group is sitting in the pub during a zombie apocalypse with nothing to do
jokes.punchline: Ed's solution for group entertainment is an orang-utan impression from a 1978 Clint Eastwood film — both the reference and the earnestness of the suggestion are funny
jokes.explanation: Ed's entertainment instincts perfectly defined: when things are dire, do an orang-utan impression. 'Has anyone seen Every Which Way But Loose?' as a preface is very funny — it's a film almost no one in the group will have seen.

jokes.text: "I'm not a performing monkey." — Ed refusing to do his impression after it's been hyped
jokes.setup: Everyone is now enthusiastically chanting 'do it, do it, do it' for Ed's orang-utan impression
jokes.punchline: Ed declines with 'I'm not a performing monkey' — which is both accidentally ironic (the impression is literally an ape) and classically performative refusal
jokes.explanation: 'I'm not a performing monkey' said by someone about to do an ape impression is a genuinely clever accidental self-contradiction. The wordplay between 'monkey' and an orang-utan impression is tight. The build-up (everyone chanting, Ed hyping it) makes the refusal funnier.

jokes.text: "What about the lights?" / "Yes. Don't advertise our whereabouts." / "The lights are on a separate circuit. Just flip the mains breakers. It's quite simple, David."
jokes.setup: Shaun figures out the power is back on and decides to watch television; David worries about lights advertising their position
jokes.punchline: Shaun confirms David's concern about lights is valid, then explains they're on a separate circuit with barely concealed condescension — 'It's quite simple, David' — reversing the usual competence dynamic
jokes.explanation: 'It's quite simple, David' has David's own condescension returned to him, which is satisfying comedy. Quick, functional, but not among the standout moments.

jokes.text: "Liz, erm... have you got a quid?" — Shaun needing to pay for the pub's wall-mounted TV
jokes.setup: The group has figured out how to watch television for distraction; Shaun is in charge
jokes.punchline: The pub TV runs on a coin-operated mechanism — requiring a quid — which Shaun doesn't have; they're in an apocalypse and he still has to ask Liz for pocket money
jokes.explanation: The coin-op TV is a perfect British pub detail and the visual comedy of needing a pound coin to watch zombie news broadcasts is excellent. Shaun asking Liz for the money is a small relationship beat that works.

jokes.text: "Never anything on, is there?" — Shaun about the apocalypse news coverage
jokes.setup: The group has just watched emergency news broadcasts about the zombie apocalypse
jokes.punchline: Shaun responds to the horrifying television coverage with the standard British complaint about nothing good being on TV — applied to zombie apocalypse broadcasting
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best deadpan lines. 'Never anything on, is there?' applied to apocalypse news is perfect British understatement — the most universal TV complaint deployed in the least applicable context. High economy (five words), universal recognition, brilliantly timed. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: 'Never anything on, is there?' — Shaun flipping through zombie-apocalypse news on TV.
jokes.setup: The power is restored; they switch on the television hoping for news about the zombie outbreak.
jokes.punchline: 'Never anything on, is there?' — the universal British complaint about bad television, applied to coverage of the actual zombie apocalypse.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. 'Never anything on, is there?' applied to zombie-apocalypse television is a masterpiece of Britishness: the country is ending and his complaint is about TV quality. The economy (six words) is extraordinary. It's simultaneously a perfect character moment, a cultural observation, and an absurdist non-sequitur. Easily 8.5 craft — it's the kind of line that becomes a cultural touchstone.

jokes.text: "They followed me." / "I thought you said you gave them the slip." / "Yeah." / "Well, we'll just have to be extra quiet then, won't we."
jokes.setup: The pub is surrounded by zombies; Shaun admits they followed him back
jokes.punchline: Shaun's breezy 'we'll just have to be extra quiet' as the solution to being surrounded by zombies is perfectly pitched British problem-minimisation
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'I thought you gave them the slip' / 'Yeah' (admission of failure dressed as confirmation) to 'we'll just be extra quiet' as a plan is an excellent deflation sequence. The confidence of 'won't we' is funny.

jokes.text: "Ed, no! Turn it off!" — Ed turns the jukebox on at maximum volume while surrounded by zombies
jokes.setup: Shaun has just said the group must be 'extra quiet' because they are surrounded by zombies; everyone goes still
jokes.punchline: Ed immediately turns on the jukebox at full volume — the most catastrophic possible response to 'be extra quiet,' executed with perfect timing as the reel's final joke
jokes.explanation: The reel's perfect button joke. The structure is flawless: Shaun says 'be extra quiet,' beat, Ed turns on the jukebox. The anticipation of what Ed might do wrong, combined with the specificity of a jukebox (classic pub fixture) is exactly right. Earns 8.8 for the structure — the entire reel has been building to exactly this kind of Ed catastrophe, and it delivers completely. The timing is the craft.

jokes.text: David is told to 'kill the Queen' and panics, then is told it's the jukebox
jokes.setup: Shaun barks urgent orders including 'David, kill the Queen' during a crisis, implying something extreme
jokes.punchline: He means the Queen jukebox, not anything violent — David's panic is the payoff
jokes.explanation: Classic Edgar Wright misdirection: the ambiguity of 'kill the Queen' in a crisis context lands perfectly, playing on both the band's name and the panic of the moment. Tight, economic, well-structured.

jokes.text: Shaun proposes using pool cues as weapons mid-crisis planning sequence to the tune of 'Don't Stop Me Now'
jokes.setup: The group debates weapons and tactics — cocktails, the rifle, flaming spirits — escalating urgency
jokes.punchline: 'How about pool?' — the mundane, pub-sport answer to a deadly zombie attack
jokes.explanation: The punchline is bathetic in the best way — after escalating tactical options, the answer is 'pool'. Works within the film's pub-as-fortress logic and pays off earlier weapon setups.

jokes.text: 'Don't Stop Me Now' plays on the jukebox as the group beats zombies with pool cues in choreographed sync with the music
jokes.setup: The jukebox is set to random and 'Don't Stop Me Now' begins — the group must kill zombies while the upbeat Queen track plays
jokes.punchline: The cheerful, euphoric song perfectly underscores increasingly violent zombie-bashing, with the group's movements syncing to the beat
jokes.explanation: One of the most celebrated sequences in British comedy cinema. The genius is multi-layered: the song's lyrics ('I'm having such a good time', 'don't stop me now') ironically comment on the horror, the choreography to the beat turns violence into dance, and the earlier setup of Ed putting the jukebox on random makes this feel earned. The sequence reaches genuine craft heights — it's cinematic joke-writing of the highest order, comparable to the vasectomy calibration anchor in terms of layered payoff and cultural impact.

jokes.text: 'Why is Queen still on?' — David's exasperated line mid-zombie fight
jokes.setup: The group is mid-combat, the Queen track is still playing
jokes.punchline: David's most pressing concern is the incongruous music, not the zombies — a perfect character beat for the uptight David
jokes.explanation: Four words that reveal everything about David's character. While chaos erupts, his pedantic concern about the music is perfectly in-character and lands as a sharp character beat mid-action.

jokes.text: 'We have a situation!' / 'I know!'
jokes.setup: Zombies are actively attacking during a Queen-soundtracked brawl
jokes.punchline: David's bureaucratic announcement of 'a situation' is so absurdly understated that Shaun's flat 'I know' deflates it further
jokes.explanation: Classic British understatement in a crisis. The word 'situation' is doing all the heavy lifting — it's office-speak dropped into a zombie apocalypse. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'Why didn't you just shoot him, man?'
jokes.setup: Shaun has just beaten a zombie to death with a pool cue in a prolonged, exhausting sequence to the finale of 'Don't Stop Me Now'
jokes.punchline: Ed's simple, logical question — why the elaborate bludgeoning when you have a gun? — punctures the heroic moment with pure laziness
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation. After a visually spectacular action sequence, Ed's one-line question exposes the absurdity of everything that just happened. It's pure Ed — lazy, logical, and puncturing any sense of heroism. Economy is near-perfect: eight words do the whole job.

jokes.text: Shaun begins 'Ed, for the last time, it's...' and trails off — he realises the gun is empty / broken / out of ammo
jokes.setup: Shaun starts to give the authoritative answer about why he couldn't use the gun
jokes.punchline: He trails off, implying he doesn't actually have a good reason — or the gun didn't work — revealing the whole bludgeoning WAS unnecessary
jokes.explanation: The ellipsis IS the joke. Shaun's inability to finish the sentence validates Ed's question retroactively and compounds the deflation of the previous beat. The trailing-off is a structurally elegant anti-punchline.

jokes.text: 'I fucking knew it! What did I tell you? Big Al was right.'
jokes.setup: An unspecified event has just confirmed something 'Big Al' predicted — in the middle of the zombie apocalypse
jokes.punchline: Ed's total vindication of the mysterious 'Big Al' in this moment, treating a pub-mate's conspiracy theory as validated by the undead apocalypse
jokes.explanation: The mysterious 'Big Al' is never explained, which makes it funnier. Ed's delight at being vindicated — and his loyalty to this unknown person's worldview — is a perfect character moment. The ambiguity is a feature, not a bug.

jokes.text: 'But dogs can look up.'
jokes.setup: A callback to an earlier argument in the film (Reel 1) about whether dogs can look up
jokes.punchline: In the middle of a zombie crisis, Ed chooses this moment to make his final, definitive point in a long-running petty argument
jokes.explanation: Five words. This is the platonic ideal of a callback joke: it pays off a seemingly throwaway early-film argument at exactly the wrong (and therefore right) moment, it requires no explanation, it is completely in character for Ed, and it lands harder on rewatch when you know it's coming. The economy score of 10 is warranted — there is not a single wasted syllable. This rivals the best jokes in the film.

jokes.text: Exchange about gun experience: 'Apart from Ed?' / 'I'm a pacifist.' / 'Apart from David and Ed?' / 'What was Ed's experience?' / 'He shot his sister in the leg.'
jokes.setup: Shaun asks who has fired a gun before as a serious tactical question
jokes.punchline: David claims pacifism (he has the gun), then we learn Ed has prior experience — having shot his sister in the leg
jokes.explanation: A beautifully escalating exchange. David's 'pacifist' claim while holding the gun is ironic gold, and the revelation that Ed's experience is shooting his own sister is a perfect dark-comedy kicker. The structure builds methodically to the best reveal.

jokes.text: 'Call them shells.' / '29 shells.'
jokes.setup: Shaun announces they have '29 bullets' in a crisis briefing
jokes.punchline: David pedantically corrects 'bullets' to 'shells' — his insufferable need to be right persisting even mid-apocalypse
jokes.explanation: Entirely about character. David's pedantry is consistent and this is a small but perfectly placed beat showing he can't stop being himself even when surrounded by zombies.

jokes.text: 'As Bertrand Russell said, the only thing that will redeem mankind is co-operation.' / 'Was that on a beer mat?' / 'Yeah, it was Guinness Extra Cold.' / 'I won't say anything.' / 'Thanks.'
jokes.setup: Shaun quotes Bertrand Russell to rally the group with a philosophical point about co-operation
jokes.punchline: He got it off a Guinness beer mat — the depth of his philosophical knowledge is exactly zero, and his sheepish confirmation is disarming
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional craft. Shaun's attempt at Churchillian leadership is immediately deflated by the revelation that his profound quote came from a beer mat — but then the specificity of 'Guinness Extra Cold' makes it even funnier. The 'I won't say anything / Thanks' exchange adds a conspiratorial warmth. It's character comedy, sitcom deflation, and Britishness all at once. Justifiably above 8.

jokes.text: 'Sorry, we're closed!' — Shaun shouts at zombies at the door
jokes.setup: Zombies are approaching the pub windows/doors in a desperate siege situation
jokes.punchline: Shaun defaults to pub-staff autopilot and tells the zombies they're closed — a completely useless but very British reflex
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfectly placed. The British instinct to announce closing time to the undead encapsulates the film's entire comic philosophy: mundane social conventions persist in the face of the apocalypse. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: 'The safety!' / 'That happened to me on stage.'
jokes.setup: David fumbles with the rifle safety in the middle of a siege — a critical tactical failure
jokes.punchline: His explanation that this happened to him 'on stage' implies he's been in some dramatic production or historical re-enactment — the specificity is absurd
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-placed beat. The implication that David has theatrical/re-enactment experience but still can't work a safety in a real crisis adds a layer of uselessness to his character. Economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: 'Three o'clock!' / 'Where?' / 'Three o'clock!' / 'Oh, over there again. Quarter to twelve.' / 'What?' / '11:45!' / 'Keep it simple!' / 'Top left!'
jokes.setup: Shaun gives military-style clock-position directions to David during the firefight
jokes.punchline: David either mishears or misunderstands, Shaun keeps reformatting his directions, the whole thing devolves into 'top left' — the system collapses into the simplest possible instruction
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured escalation joke. The logic collapses in real-time as Shaun attempts increasing specificity ('quarter to twelve', '11:45') before giving up entirely with 'top left'. The absurdist ratcheting of a simple problem is very Wright — tight, smart, and actioned perfectly.

jokes.text: 'It's been a funny sort of day, hasn't it?'
jokes.setup: Barbara is dying from a zombie bite, an emotionally devastating scene — the worst day of multiple characters' lives
jokes.punchline: Her British understatement of a zombie apocalypse as 'a funny sort of day' is both heartbreaking and genuinely funny
jokes.explanation: One of the great single lines in British comedy cinema. The genius is that it functions simultaneously as genuine comedy AND genuine pathos — Barbara is not being funny deliberately, she's being herself, and 'herself' is a person of such profound, unshakeable English decorum that she understates her own death. The economy is perfect: seven words carry the entire weight of her character. The line is quotable, devastating, and funny all at once. This is what 9+ craft looks like.

jokes.text: David announces 'I'm gonna count to three' to threaten Shaun about shooting Barbara, then counts — 'One... two... three!' — and does nothing
jokes.setup: David draws the gun on the group, says he's going to count to three in a show of authority
jokes.punchline: He reaches three and nothing happens — his authority evaporates instantly, exposing him as all bluster
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony. The countdown structure primes audience expectation of action; the deflation when nothing happens is perfectly timed and consistent with David's character as someone who talks big and delivers nothing.

jokes.text: 'Ed, don't exacerbate things!' / 'What's that mean?'
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to de-escalate an explosive confrontation between David and Shaun
jokes.punchline: Ed has no idea what 'exacerbate' means — his genuine, unhelpful confusion undercuts the drama at exactly the wrong moment
jokes.explanation: Ed's intellectual limitations have been consistent throughout the film. This beat doesn't surprise but it's well-placed — his genuine confusion deflates an emotionally intense scene with a quick puncture. Character-consistent and economic.

jokes.text: 'That's what this is about, isn't it? He doesn't like me! He's always hated me and now he wants to shoot my mum.'
jokes.setup: David makes a rational argument about Barbara turning into a zombie and being a danger to everyone
jokes.punchline: Shaun reframes the entirely logical zombie threat as a personal grudge — 'he wants to shoot my mum' — a stunning act of emotional illogic
jokes.explanation: Funny because it's true to how grief works — people deflect rational arguments into personal grievances. 'He wants to shoot my mum' is an absurd but emotionally coherent reading of the situation. The illogic is the joke.

jokes.text: 'We all know you're in love with Liz.' / 'That is not true.' / 'Yes it is!' — David forced to deny romantic feelings mid-zombie apocalypse
jokes.setup: An argument about whether to shoot zombie Barbara has somehow escalated into Shaun accusing David of secretly being in love with Liz
jokes.punchline: The completely inappropriate relationship drama erupts mid-siege — David's denials land as confirmation
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of romantic jealousy with the zombie siege is excellent cringe comedy. The scene perfectly mirrors how real arguments spiral from practical disagreements into emotional grievances — amplified to absurdity by the apocalyptic stakes.

jokes.text: 'I've come to terms with that, Daffs, why can't you?'
jokes.setup: Shaun accuses David of only befriending him to get closer to Liz, then being 'there to pick up the pieces' when rejected
jokes.punchline: Shaun's breezy 'I've come to terms with that' — delivered as though it's perfectly normal for his best mate to have used him as romantic collateral — is extraordinary self-deprecation
jokes.explanation: Shaun's capacity for emotional compartmentalisation is a consistent character trait. The fact that he's 'come to terms with' being used as a romantic stepping stone — and finds it puzzling that David hasn't — is a surprising character reveal delivered with perfect economy.

jokes.text: 'David! There are slightly more pressing matters at hand here.'
jokes.setup: David is mid-romantic declaration during a zombie siege
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'slightly more pressing matters' is the most restrained possible rebuke — 'slightly' is doing enormous work here as an understatement
jokes.explanation: The word 'slightly' in 'slightly more pressing matters' is a beautiful understatement. Liz doesn't rage or lecture — she just says the word 'slightly' and lets it do the work. Very economical.

jokes.text: 'Like "Daffs" pointing a gun at my mum.' / 'I'm not being unreasonable, "Pickle".'
jokes.setup: David and Shaun are in a tense standoff; Shaun sarcastically uses David's nickname for Dianne
jokes.punchline: David retaliates using Shaun's pet name 'Pickle' — the sniping juvenile nickname exchange in the middle of a deadly crisis
jokes.explanation: The pet-name sniping is a sharp piece of character writing. 'Pickle' especially lands because it's such a soft, unmasculine nickname being wielded as a rhetorical weapon. The childishness of the exchange is precisely calibrated.

jokes.text: 'You've gone from a chartered accountant to Charlton Heston.' / 'I'm not a chartered accountant.' / 'Well, you look like one.' / 'Yeah.' / 'I'm a lecturer.' / 'You're a twat.'
jokes.setup: Liz is criticising David for taking up the gun and acting like an action hero
jokes.punchline: The 'chartered accountant / Charlton Heston' alliteration lands as a sharp insult; David's correction ('I'm a lecturer') is immediately countered by Ed's perfect one-word verdict: 'You're a twat.'
jokes.explanation: The alliterative 'chartered accountant / Charlton Heston' insult is genuinely clever — both are square men who look right in a suit, and the alliteration gives it snap. But the kicker is the exchange about his job: David's pedantic self-correction ('I'm a lecturer') opens the door for Ed's flat 'You're a twat,' which arrives like a perfect punchline. The setup/deflation/kicker three-beat structure is excellent craft. Ed does nothing all film and delivers the best single-word verdict possible.

jokes.text: 'We're not using the Z word.'
jokes.setup: David says 'zombie' to describe what Barbara will become
jokes.punchline: Even now — mid-siege, his mother dying — Shaun maintains his ban on the word 'zombie', a running gag from throughout the film
jokes.explanation: The running gag lands with extra weight here because the stakes are so high — Barbara is dying of a zombie bite and Shaun is still policing vocabulary. The juxtaposition of trivial wordplay against maximum emotional stakes is perfectly Wright. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: 'Even if he is being a twat.' / 'Yep.'
jokes.setup: Liz diplomatically begins to mediate — 'I can see what David is trying to say...'
jokes.punchline: She immediately qualifies this with 'even if he is being a twat' and David's resigned 'Yep' is a perfect self-aware concession
jokes.explanation: David's self-aware 'Yep' to being called a twat is the best part. It signals that even David knows he's been impossible, and his quiet agreement is both funny and strangely sympathetic.

jokes.text: 'Well... I think we're all agreed, you did the right thing there.'
jokes.setup: Shaun has just been forced to shoot his zombifying mother — a moment of profound, genuine tragedy
jokes.punchline: Ed's matter-of-fact verdict on the situation, delivered like a panel reviewing a mild workplace decision
jokes.explanation: Ed's ability to offer managerial consensus-speak ('I think we're all agreed') after the most emotionally devastating act of the film is an extraordinary tone shift. It works because it's simultaneously the wrong thing to say and, in Ed's mind, a genuine attempt at comfort. The phrasing is impeccably British. Justifies 8+ for its dark wit and perfect character voice.

jokes.text: 'After where he led us?' — accusation directed at Shaun about his leadership during the zombie apocalypse
jokes.setup: David argues for leaving the pub, suggesting Shaun's leadership has been poor
jokes.punchline: The full indictment of Shaun's plan — which was 'go to the pub' — being described as disastrous leadership is both fair and funny
jokes.explanation: A mild laugh at best — the joke is diffuse and relies on the audience remembering the original plan. It's functionally ironic but not punchy enough to elevate beyond a smirk.

jokes.text: 'I'm so sorry, Dianne.' / 'Maybe I'm not the one you should be apologising to.'
jokes.setup: David, having caused chaos, apologises to his girlfriend Dianne
jokes.punchline: Dianne implies he should apologise to Shaun instead — but the moment lands with dark irony given what's about to happen to David
jokes.explanation: Gains significant rewatch value because David is about to die without having made amends, making Dianne's redirection tragically ironic. In the moment, it's a functional beat; on rewatch, it stings.

jokes.text: 'Oh dear.' — said as Dianne dives out after David into the zombie horde
jokes.setup: Dianne watches David being torn apart by zombies and leaps through the broken window to try to save him — a suicidal act of devotion
jokes.punchline: 'Oh dear' — two words, maximum understatement, peak Ed
jokes.explanation: Possibly the most economical joke in the film. Two syllables to respond to two people being eaten by zombies. The genius is in the specificity: 'Oh dear' is what you'd say if someone spilled a cup of tea. Ed's flat affect in the face of carnage is perfectly crystallised. Economy is essentially perfect — you couldn't say less and still have a joke. High character integration: this is exactly what Ed would say.

jokes.text: 'Oh dear.' — reaction to David being torn apart by zombies
jokes.setup: David has been pulled through the window and is being graphically dismembered by zombies
jokes.punchline: Ed's two-word response — 'Oh dear' — is the most understated possible reaction to watching someone be torn apart
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum impact. 'Oh dear' is the British equivalent of shrugging at an atrocity. Ed has never liked David, and his muted response to the most horrific death possible is perfectly in character — not cruel, just utterly indifferent. The economy is flawless. Comparable in brevity and darkness to the best deadpan one-liners in British comedy.

jokes.text: 'Shauny, look who it is.' / 'Fuck-a-doodle-doo!'
jokes.setup: In the chaos of the final siege, Ed spots zombie Pete — Shaun's hated flatmate from the beginning of the film
jokes.punchline: 'Fuck-a-doodle-doo!' — Ed's invented expletive-portmanteau, which is a callback to its use earlier in the film, used here to greet the zombie version of Pete
jokes.explanation: A double callback: the return of zombie Pete (a fully set-up character from the opening act) AND Ed's coined expletive 'Fuck-a-doodle-doo' returning at peak chaos. The invented word is the kind of thing that becomes beloved — it's funny on first use, funnier on callback, and deeply character-specific. High quotability and rewatch value.

jokes.text: 'Don't groan at me, you thick fuck!'
jokes.setup: Zombie Pete presumably groans at Ed (as zombies do)
jokes.punchline: Ed responds as though Pete's zombie-groan is a personal insult — specifically, an accusation of stupidity — and defends himself against it
jokes.explanation: Ed interpreting a zombie groan as a targeted insult about his intelligence, and responding defensively, is a perfect character beat. The relationship between Ed and Pete — always adversarial — continues even in Pete's undead form. Character-specific and very funny.

jokes.text: 'What?' / 'Chuck us a cloth, will you?' — Ed, having been bitten, calmly asks for a cloth
jokes.setup: Ed has been bitten by a zombie — a death sentence in this world — in the middle of frantic chaos
jokes.punchline: Ed's first request post-bite is for a cloth — entirely practical, entirely Ed, completely unbothered by his own impending death
jokes.explanation: Among the film's best character moments. Ed has been bitten — he's going to die, and he knows it — and his only concern is cleaning up. 'Chuck us a cloth, will you?' is so utterly, perfectly Ed that it's both heartbreaking and hilarious. The character integration score of 9.5 is warranted: no other character in this film (or many others) would respond to a zombie bite with a housekeeping request. This is exceptional writing.

jokes.text: 'That's it then, we're trapped. "Hey, let's go to the Winchester!" Whose fucking idea was that?'
jokes.setup: The cellar escape hatch won't open — they are trapped
jokes.punchline: Liz's sarcastically quoted 'Hey, let's go to the Winchester!' throws the entire film's premise back at Shaun — the plan was always catastrophically bad
jokes.explanation: Full-film callback that lands perfectly. Liz's impression of Shaun is biting, the irony is total, and 'Whose fucking idea was that?' lands as both a genuine frustration and a meta-comment on the film's entire plot logic. High quotability because it encapsulates the film's comic premise in a single line.

jokes.text: 'Man, I've really ballsed this up.'
jokes.setup: Shaun takes stock: his mum is dead, two friends are dead, they're trapped in a cellar surrounded by zombies
jokes.punchline: 'I've really ballsed this up' — the most British, mild self-assessment of a catastrophic chain of failures
jokes.explanation: Classic British understatement. Shaun's self-criticism is both accurate and fantastically mild given the scale of the disaster. Consistent with his character and lands a solid laugh in a dark stretch.

jokes.text: 'I suppose we could take a few of them out if they stand in a line.'
jokes.setup: Shaun calculates they have two shells left with hordes of zombies approaching
jokes.punchline: His optimistic tactical suggestion — if only the zombies would helpfully queue up — is both absurd and oddly plausible given the film's zombie logic
jokes.explanation: The image of politely queuing zombies is a very British absurdism. Shaun's optimistic arithmetic in the face of certain doom is in perfect character, and 'if they stand in a line' is a wonderful detail.

jokes.text: 'I wasn't thinking about them.' / 'I know.'
jokes.setup: Shaun has suggested using the last two shells on zombies; Liz indicates she was thinking of using them on themselves
jokes.punchline: The quiet, mutual acknowledgement that they were discussing suicide is handled with such understatement it functions as both dark comedy and genuine tenderness
