jokes.explanation: Four words total, and they carry enormous weight. The understated 'I know' implies Shaun had been thinking the same thing. The dark comedy here is inseparable from genuine emotion — the joke only works because the relationship between Shaun and Liz feels real.

jokes.text: 'What about Ed? There's only two shells.' / 'I don't mind being eaten.'
jokes.setup: Shaun realises the two-shell suicide plan doesn't account for Ed
jokes.punchline: Ed graciously volunteers to be eaten by zombies — his breezy self-sacrifice is both moving and absurdly casual
jokes.explanation: One of the great Ed lines. 'I don't mind being eaten' has the same quality as the best deadpan in the film — it's simultaneously absurd, in-character, and genuinely touching. Ed has always been the character who takes up the least space and demands the least; of course he would volunteer to be eaten so his friends can die more cleanly. The line combines dark comedy with sincere character revelation. Justifies 8.5+.

jokes.text: 'I don't think I've got it in me to shoot my flatmate, my mum and my girlfriend all in the same evening.'
jokes.setup: The group is discussing who will shoot whom in a mercy-killing arrangement
jokes.punchline: Shaun lists 'flatmate, mum and girlfriend' as an administrative concern — the sheer accumulation of loved ones he's already had to kill (or is being asked to kill) becomes the joke
jokes.explanation: The list structure ('flatmate, mum and girlfriend') is excellent comedy construction. Individually each loss is tragic; listed together as a scheduling inconvenience, they become a dark comedy inventory. The 'all in the same evening' qualifier is the kicker — as if spread across a week it would have been manageable. Consistently quoted, genuinely clever.

jokes.text: 'What makes you think I've taken you back?'
jokes.setup: Shaun has listed his 'girlfriend' as one of the people he doesn't want to shoot — implicitly treating them as reconciled
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately contests this assumption — even facing death, their relationship status is unresolved and she won't let it slide
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing in a scene that's teetering between dark comedy and genuine pathos. Liz's refusal to let the relationship-status assumption stand — in a cellar surrounded by zombies, contemplating suicide — is a great character beat. The specificity is key: she's not angry, just precise. 'What makes you think I've taken you back?' is very quotable and genuinely funny.

jokes.text: 'Well... you don't want to die single, do you?'
jokes.setup: Liz has just contested their relationship status while facing death
jokes.punchline: Shaun's argument for reconciliation is purely practical: dying single is worse. It's a romantic argument stripped to its laziest possible logic
jokes.explanation: Shaun's romantic logic at its laziest and funniest: 'you don't want to die single' is a terrible reason to get back with someone and a completely Shaun reason. The economy is excellent and the character specificity is high. It's also a sweet beat — his clumsiness is endearing even here.

jokes.text: 'I haven't had a fag since yesterday, I promise.' / 'He hasn't.'
jokes.setup: Shaun is trying to convince Liz he's changed, citing not smoking as evidence
jokes.punchline: Ed immediately and flatly contradicts him — 'He hasn't' — with no hesitation, no elaboration
jokes.explanation: Ed's flat 'He hasn't' is a devastating two-word contradiction. The timing — Shaun is mid-romantic-pitch — and the total lack of loyalty from his best friend make it land perfectly. Ed doesn't editorialize, doesn't qualify, doesn't apologize: he just states the fact. Character comedy at its most economical.

jokes.text: 'Maybe we should have one now.' — suggesting having a cigarette while contemplating suicide in a zombie-besieged cellar
jokes.setup: Liz and Shaun have established there are no cigarettes; they are trapped and potentially about to die
jokes.punchline: Liz suggesting 'maybe we should have one now' — a last cigarette before facing death — is both funny and unexpectedly sweet
jokes.explanation: The 'last cigarette' tradition before execution, applied to a zombie apocalypse, is a gentle dark comedy beat. It also signals Liz warming to Shaun again — her participation in the ritual is an acceptance of sorts. Economical and tonally right.

jokes.text: 'You left them in my flat.' / 'Yeah, in the bin.' / 'I was desperate.' / 'Sneaky monkey.' / 'Sorry.' / 'I won't say anything.'
jokes.setup: Liz discovers Shaun retrieved cigarettes from her bin after claiming to have quit
jokes.punchline: 'Sneaky monkey' as Liz's affectionate scolding, and 'I won't say anything' — the same phrase used earlier for the beer mat Bertrand Russell quote — lands as a callback and a character-warming moment
jokes.explanation: A gentle scene of domestic bickering transplanted into an apocalypse. 'Sneaky monkey' is an odd, specifically British term of affection that reveals a lot about Liz and Shaun's relationship. The repeated 'I won't say anything' adds cohesion to the reel.

jokes.text: 'I only hold you back.' / 'Yeah, but...'
jokes.setup: Ed is suggesting Shaun and Liz leave without him; he says he only holds Shaun back
jokes.punchline: Shaun's 'Yeah, but...' — he doesn't deny it, just trails off — is a genuine and funny acknowledgement of Ed's honest self-assessment
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'Yeah, but...' contains the whole joke — Shaun can't actually disagree with Ed's self-assessment, and the honesty between them is funnier and more moving than a denial would be.

jokes.text: 'I only hold you back.' — Ed's decision to stay behind, delivered with simple, complete sincerity
jokes.setup: Ed is bitten and cannot leave; he encourages Shaun and Liz to escape without him
jokes.punchline: 'I only hold you back' — said as a matter of fact, not self-pity. Ed has genuine insight into his own limitation for the first time, delivered straight
jokes.explanation: More affecting than funny, but functions as dark comedy because it's both perfectly true (Ed has held Shaun back throughout) and heartbreaking. The simplicity is the craft.

jokes.text: 'Ed, I'm sorry.' / 'What for?'
jokes.setup: Shaun apologises to Ed in an emotional farewell
jokes.punchline: Ed has no idea what Shaun could possibly be apologising for — suggesting either genuine innocence or total lack of self-awareness about his behaviour throughout the film
jokes.explanation: Ed's 'What for?' is funny because it implies zero awareness of the conflict Shaun has been managing around him all film. It also suggests total unconditionality — from Ed's perspective, there's nothing to apologise for because he doesn't hold any of it against Shaun.

jokes.text: 'I'm sorry too.' / 'It's OK.' / 'No... I'm sorry, Shaun.' — Ed's zombie groan in farewell
jokes.setup: Ed and Shaun have an emotional reconciliation; Shaun accepts Ed's apology — then Ed makes a zombie groan
jokes.punchline: Ed's groan mid-reconciliation signals the bite is taking hold — but played as a beat in a sincere conversation, it lands as both a shock and a dark laugh
jokes.explanation: The structural move of inserting the first zombie symptom inside a sincere emotional beat is clever screenwriting. It recontextualizes Ed's last 'No... I'm sorry, Shaun' — is it heartfelt or is it already the zombie talking? The ambiguity enriches both the comedy and the drama.

jokes.text: 'Oh God! That's not funny.' / 'I'll stop doing 'em when you stop laughing.' / 'I'm not laughing.'
jokes.setup: Ed has been bitten and is turning into a zombie; he's apparently making zombie noises/faces at Shaun as a joke
jokes.punchline: He refuses to stop making zombie impressions until Shaun stops laughing — Shaun denies he's laughing — the whole thing is both deeply sweet and deeply inappropriate
jokes.explanation: One of the best moments in the film. Ed spending his last human moments doing zombie impressions to make Shaun laugh — and Shaun helplessly laughing despite himself — is a perfect encapsulation of their friendship. It's funny, it's sad, and it's completely in character. The 'I'm not laughing' denial seals it. This is what friendship looks like in an Edgar Wright film.

jokes.text: 'Bye, Ed. Love you.' / 'Cheers.' / 'I love you too, man.' / 'Gay.'
jokes.setup: Shaun and Ed say a genuine, emotional farewell — 'love you'
jokes.punchline: 'Gay.' — Ed's final word to Shaun is a laddish deflection from the sincerity of the moment, perfectly in character
jokes.explanation: Perfect ending to the Ed and Shaun relationship arc. The progression — Shaun says 'love you', Ed says 'cheers' (can't quite reciprocate directly), then admits 'I love you too, man', then immediately undercuts it with 'Gay' — is an entire character in four words. The 'Gay' deflection is both a laugh and a devastating character truth: Ed can only express genuine love by immediately making a joke of it. One of the most memorable exits in British film comedy. Economy score of 10 is warranted.

jokes.text: 'Yvonne?' — Shaun recognises Yvonne (his counterpart character) among the army rescue party
jokes.setup: Throughout the film, Yvonne has been Shaun's parallel — doing a competent version of everything Shaun does badly
jokes.punchline: Of course Yvonne made it — she organised the military rescue; Shaun's stunned recognition ('Yvonne?') is both a callback and a commentary on his own inadequacy
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Yvonne parallel subplot is satisfying — she went the military/sensible route while Shaun went to the pub. 'Well, glad somebody made it' as her greeting is a nicely understated put-down.

jokes.text: 'How are you doing?' / 'Surviving.' — Shaun's reunion with Yvonne, his parallel-universe counterpart
jokes.setup: Shaun is rescued after the zombie siege; Yvonne asks how he's doing
jokes.punchline: 'Surviving.' — a word that is literally true (zombie apocalypse) and also means 'barely getting by' in everyday usage; the double meaning lands with dark wit
jokes.explanation: One word doing double duty as literal and figurative meaning. The irony is clean and economical. Not exceptional but well-executed.

jokes.text: 'Is it just the two of you?' — Yvonne's question after Shaun's group has been catastrophically reduced
jokes.setup: Shaun left with a group of six; he returns with just Liz
jokes.punchline: Yvonne's simple question lands as a devastating audit of the casualties — 'just the two of you' says everything about how badly it went
jokes.explanation: Functional dark-comedy beat. The understatement of the question does the work — no elaboration needed. Not particularly crafted but lands in context.

jokes.text: 'Well, glad somebody made it.' — Yvonne's reaction to meeting Shaun
jokes.setup: It's clear the rescue group expected few survivors; Yvonne acknowledges Shaun made it
jokes.punchline: 'Glad somebody made it' has a weary, low-expectations quality — the bar for success has been set at mere survival
jokes.explanation: Mild beat. It's functional and tonally appropriate but doesn't rise above understatement-as-default. The writing isn't doing much beyond acknowledging the situation.

jokes.text: Post-apocalypse TV montage: newsreaders discussing zombies in ordinary broadcast formats — 'Zombaid', zombie service industry recruitment, zombie sports commentary
jokes.setup: Six months after Z-Day; the world has returned to normal and zombies are being integrated into society
jokes.punchline: Zombies are used in the service industry; there is a charity called 'Zombaid'; a zombie falling over is sports entertainment; a woman is still married to her zombie husband
jokes.explanation: The montage is conceptually brilliant — the film's central satirical joke (humans are already zombies; nothing will really change) paid off in the final act. Each individual element (Band Aid parody, service-industry zombies, zombie sports, zombie marriage) is an independent gag and they accumulate into a devastating social satire. 'Zombaid' especially is a perfect one-word joke. This is counted as one composite moment but contains multiple micro-gags.

jokes.text: Sports commentary: 'He can't quite get it. Ooh! He's fallen, he's down!' — a zombie stumbling in what is implied to be a sporting event
jokes.setup: Society has normalised zombies to the point of incorporating them into entertainment
jokes.punchline: A zombie athlete falling over is treated with straight sports commentary — the same breathless concern for a zombie's athletic performance as for any human competitor
jokes.explanation: The concept is funny — zombie sport — but we get it at the description level rather than seeing the full visual. Works as part of the montage rather than as a standalone moment.

jokes.text: 'I don't see nothing wrong with it but I know that some people would. But he's my husband, you know. I still love him and I got the ring.' / 'You go to bed with it?' / ''Course I do.'
jokes.setup: The TV documentary interviews a woman still in a relationship with her zombie husband
jokes.punchline: She goes to bed with her zombie husband and wears the ring — the mundane persistence of domestic life through zombie transformation is both deeply unsettling and very funny
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier documentary clips. The idea that someone would maintain a marriage with a zombie — not out of denial but as a genuine ongoing choice — is a great dark-comedy concept. ''Course I do' has the authentic ring of a real documentary subject defending a life choice others find bizarre.

jokes.text: Chat show interview: 'I don't see nothing wrong with it but I know that some people would. But he's my husband, you know. I still love him and I got the ring.' / 'You go to bed with it?' / 'Course I do.'
jokes.setup: Society has normalised zombies; a chat show features people discussing their relationships with zombie loved ones
jokes.punchline: A woman is still maintaining her marriage to her zombie husband — going to bed with him, wearing the ring — treating her undead husband as a continuing partner
jokes.explanation: Dark and funny — the Mrs. Brown's Boys or Jerry Springer framing of zombie marriage is an inspired sociological joke. 'Course I do' about sharing a bed with a zombie husband is the right tone of indignant normalcy. Part of the montage's satirical argument about how society domesticates horror.

jokes.text: Shaun and Liz's new domestic routine: 'a cup of tea, get the Sundays, head down the Phoenix for a roast, veg out in the pub, wander home, watch a bit of telly, go to bed'
jokes.setup: Post-apocalypse, life has returned to normal; Shaun lays out the Sunday plan
jokes.punchline: The plan is exactly the kind of lazy, pub-centred Sunday that caused Liz to break up with Shaun at the start of the film — nothing has changed
jokes.explanation: The film's thesis statement as punchline. Wright and Pegg's whole argument is that nothing really changes — people are already the undead, shuffling through routines — and Shaun's identical Sunday plan post-apocalypse proves it. The structure of the entire film is the setup; this is the punchline. It's also genuinely warming because Liz is now fine with it. 'Perfik' as Liz's response is a lovely character beat.

jokes.text: 'Can I have two sugars, please?' / 'Ooh! Adventurous.'
jokes.setup: Liz offers to make tea; Shaun requests two sugars
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'Ooh! Adventurous.' treats the request for two sugars as a daring lifestyle choice — post-apocalypse, two sugars is boldness
jokes.explanation: Light and warm. The joke reestablishes domestic intimacy — the apocalypse is over, they're bantering about tea. 'Adventurous' applied to sugar quantity is a nicely calibrated bit of British irony.

jokes.text: 'Player two has entered the game.' — text on screen as Shaun opens the garden shed
jokes.setup: Shaun has chained zombie Ed in the garden shed; the film has established their friendship in terms of gaming
jokes.punchline: The video-game text overlay — 'Player two has entered the game' — reframes Ed's zombie existence as a continuation of his and Shaun's gaming relationship; nothing, not even zombification, ends this friendship
jokes.explanation: The perfect ending beat for the Shaun/Ed arc. The 'Player two' framing is a callback to the film's consistent use of gaming as the language of their friendship, now applied to Ed's zombie existence. It's funny, it's sweet, it's elegant, and it pays off two hours of setup in five words. The craft is exceptional: one text overlay does the work of an entire scene. The film earns its ending here. This is the film's highest-craft single joke — a 9.5.
